★★ IF YOU READ ONLY THIS — three things, in order

1 — The desk was switched on for 3.4% of the week, and that was probably right. Six gates over a 120-hour trading week is 720 available gate-hours; the desk used 24h 31m. The tournament took three signals all week, all inside one fifty-one-minute window on Friday afternoon, and won all three for $330.00. The case that this was discipline rather than cowardice is measured, not asserted: every suppressed signal was collapsed to 187 distinct impulses, repriced tick-by-tick on each gate's own live exit, and the benched set comes to +$810 saved over 127 signals. But a bootstrap puts P(the true saving is zero or worse) at 0.13, so keep the policy and stop quoting the number. HOLD #1.

2 — The router's dominant error is no longer direction. It is LATENESS. Friday's one deliberate arm was right — four lots, four winners, +$181.50 — and it was 8m 37s late, which cost $33.84 on one lot measured from the gate's own earlier suppressed signal, and $205–$705 measured from the router's side. Actuation is not the problem: the gates filled 1.4 seconds after the switch flipped. About 15 of the 20 minutes is the router's own confirmation appetite. MONDAY #2.

3 — ★ And the structural finding, which outranks both. For three cycles this report has closed with “detection is solved, selection is not” without being able to say why. Movement 3 measured it on 52,937 minutes across 41 days: against a fixed POINT threshold every precursor we own looks predictive (AUC to 0.81, p=0.00) — and once the threshold is expressed in ATR, or ATR is simply held fixed, every one of them collapses to a coin flip or below. A 55-point move is easy on a wide tape and hard on a quiet one, so anything correlated with ATR scores well against a point threshold. The desk's entire precursor toolkit is one volatility meter, and we have been asking it for a direction. BUILD #3.

★ THE SCORECARD — what survived the week

Lead with what survived the skeptic, never with the biggest number. Nine results carried real weight out of this week; here is where each one landed and the test that decided it. ★ Every row below comes from a section that RAN this cycle — nothing on this scorecard is sourced from the three sections carrying a stale banner.

The claimVerdict, and the test that decided it Where
Every precursor feature on this desk is a proxy for ATR — which is why selection keeps failing SURVIVED — the week's most important result 52,937 minutes, 41 days. Against a fixed POINT threshold, volume z, trade-count z, ATR expansion, aggressor flow, ER(15) and ATR level all beat a coin flip with p = 0.00, ATR level reaching 0.81. Express the same threshold in ATR and the discrimination inverts — ATR expansion falls to 0.234 and ATR level to 0.306, both now worse than chance. Hold ATR fixed and ask within the band and everything sits between 0.29 and 0.56. It is the same instrument measured twice: a 55-point move is easy on a wide tape and hard on a quiet one.

The three things this week actually taught the desk

1 · A precursor that predicts SIZE is not a precursor that predicts a MOVE. Every feature this desk uses to decide whether something is about to happen turns out to be measuring how volatile the tape already is. It scored beautifully for months against a fixed point threshold and it collapses the instant that threshold is normalised by ATR. The lesson generalises past this one study: if a feature and your outcome threshold are both scaled by the same hidden variable, you are measuring the variable.

2 · A win rate is not a sample size. The tournament went 6 for 6 this week. It was three gates agreeing about one push, each booking two lots of a scale-out — one market event, sampled six times. Every quantitative claim in Part 1 is deliberately built on populations of 30–130 signals instead, and the section says so in its own second paragraph. The same error in a different coat is the shadow board, where nine “independent” green arms are nine exits on one signal.

3 · The instruments fail SILENTLY, and they fail in the direction of reassurance. Three separate examples this week, none of which errored: a router blind for 3h35m while systemctl, the trial log and the tick count all read clean; two nightly rollups with no timer that simply stopped being written; two shadow A/Bs that report a perfect null because one arm never diverged. A number that arrives without a failure mode is not a measurement — and note that all three of these were found by the report, not by the monitoring.

Standing caveats on every dollar on this card

Every repriced number is a CEILING. Fills are modelled at the exact stop/target/trail level with no slippage, and the desk's own standing finding is that live losses run 1.1–3.1× modelled. Treat the policy as the edge and the headline dollar as decoration. Anything on thin n is flagged in-row as a direction, not a measurement.

The fee is $1.50 per round trip and the multipliers are not the same. MNQ is $2.00 a point; MGC is $10.00. Every gold number in Movement 3 and in Part 2.5 Part A is priced at the gold multiplier — pricing gold with the Nasdaq one would understate it fivefold, and doing the reverse would flatter it fivefold.

Six method wounds are open and they bound everything above. SUPPRESSED-OPEN is logged at tournament.py:306 and the 55-second absorption veto runs at tournament.py:360 — afterwards. So for four of the six gates the benched population Part 1 reprices contains trades the gate’s own veto would have thrown away, which makes the +$810 saving an UPPER BOUND rather than a point estimate. The two gates measured clean are grind_long and capitulation_long — HOLD #1. The entire bench replay is IN-SAMPLE by construction — it reprices decisions already made, on the tape they were made on — and every replayed figure is one lot on the Lot-A ruler while the live desk runs two, so the Lot-B tail is not modelled anywhere — HOLD #1. Neither nightly rollup has ever had a timer. router_nightly last wrote 2026-08-14 and selector_nightly 2026-08-18, so every nightly number in Part 2.6 is a rebuild done during this report, not the output of a monitor that was watching — SATURDAY #1. The router was blind for 3h35m across 43 fail-closed aborts, and systemctl, the trial log and the tick count all read clean straight through it — so “the router decided X” is, on this week’s evidence, sometimes “the router did not run” — SATURDAY #2. Two shadow A/B pairs are byte-identical (29/29 and 251/251 trades) and four arm names on the leaderboard carry one trade set, so any reading of those as independent confirmations inflates the evidence four-fold — and a broken arm reports a PERFECT NULL, which is the one failure that looks like a clean result — BUILD #5. there was no trend day. All five sessions closed with a whole-day efficiency ratio between 0.017 and 0.032, 61.5% of tradeable minutes were chop, and at least four recommendations in this report are explicitly ungradeable until one trend week lands — BUILD #8.

What did not run this cycle, named exactly. The overnight run finished 5 of its 13 body phases. Three sections were SKIPPED before they started, each allocated 19 minutes against a 20-minute floor: rehab (Part 1.5), day_rider (Part 1.6) and part25_musings (Part 2.5). Two of those three were rebuilt afterwards — Part 1.6 at 07:52Z and Part 2.5 at 08:53Z on 2026-08-29 — and every number in them is this week’s; the action card draws eight plays from the two of them. Only Part 1.5 (Rehabilitation) still carries last cycle’s text, under a red dated banner, and that text is about the week to 2026-08-21. Two more phases ran and were killed before writing their fragment (movement2_idle at 21.1 minutes, movement3 at 25.5) — but both had already written their labs to disk, so Movement 2 and Movement 3 were rebuilt from those artifacts and every number in them is this week’s. ★ REV2 — and so was the GOLD hunt. gf_MGC was killed at 23:58:08Z after writing four artifacts, and Rev 1 of this report carried no gold greenfield section at all while three other places pointed at gf_MGC as though it were present. § The evidence behind those plays

Everything from here down is the working. Two halves, one document. It opens with Part 0, which answers the only question that survives past Friday — are we getting better? — day by day, green or red, straight off the books. Then the warm half: what the live desk actually did (Part 1, with the run charts inside it — every fill of the week marked on its own session’s price path, which is the fastest way to see what the prose is describing). Then Rehabilitation (Part 1.5), where every red thing is walked through the full treatment instead of benched at face value, and the day rider (Part 1.6), the second book on the same IB account. Then the shadow board and the promotion battery (Part 2), the mid-week leads re-run adversarially (Part 2.5), and the Router Operation Review (Part 2.6). Then the cold, tape-first half: we ignore everything the desk did and ask, from the raw tape and order book, where was the money and did we show up? — on MNQ and on gold (M1) — then test whether the gates we already own could have caught the runs we missed (M2), and finally build gates from scratch and backtest them to death, the ones that failed included, that being the point (M3). Plain English, honest money, every claim a table — and every reprice a ceiling.

★★ ONE OF THOSE SECTIONS DID NOT REGENERATE THIS CYCLE, AND IT SAYS SO IN RED AT THE TOP OF ITSELF. The overnight run finished 5 of its 13 body phases. Part 1.5, Part 1.6 and Part 2.5 were all skipped before they started — each allocated 19 minutes against a 20-minute floor — but Part 1.6 and Part 2.5 were rebuilt afterwards and are this week’s. Part 1.5 (Rehabilitation) is the one that was not, so what appears under that heading is last cycle’s text, reproduced in full under a dated banner. It describes the week to 2026-08-21. Read it as prior-week context and nothing more: where it disagrees with a fresh section the fresh section wins, and no play on the action card is sourced from it. (Movement 2 and Movement 3 were killed the same way but had already written their labs to disk, so both were rebuilt from this cycle’s own artifacts and are fresh. Movement 3’s appendix carries four cluster dossiers the ISO-week rotation deliberately did not schedule — those are labelled as such, and every candidate they produced is forward-tested on new tape in §5.)

The rule behind all of that: a gap is never a null result. “We looked and found nothing” and “nobody looked” are opposite instructions for next week, so nothing is silently omitted and nothing stale is silently stitched.

What changed underneath. The Claude-run router went live 2026-07-30, mid-W31 — the first green week is the one it landed in. Its measured effect is on the tail and the frequency of red days, not their depth: the worst day before it was -1,513.00, the worst since is -2,149.44, and green days went from 2 of 12 to 12 of 23. The day-rider joined on 08-06 as a second, slower engine, and it is no longer unbeaten: -1,576.94 across 26 legs in the most recent week, of which -2,149.44 landed on Monday 08-24 alone. P1 THE LIVE DESK — Monday 24 to Friday 28 August 2026

Garrath — the six-gate tournament took three signals in the whole week and won all three. Six lots, +$330.00 net of fees, every single one of them opened inside a fifty-one minute window on Friday afternoon. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday it did not trade at all, and nor had it since 19 August — a nine-day drought. So the P&L is not the story and I am not going to dress it up as one. The story is that the desk was switched on for 3.7% of the available gate-time, the money all came from the other book, and the single largest item on the week is a −$2,149.44 position that nobody chose to hold. What follows is what I could prove, what I could only bound, and one number this desk has been quoting that does not survive its own robustness rule.

★★ If you read nothing else — five things, in order

1. What survived, cleanly. The router made exactly one deliberate momentum arm all week — Friday 14:45:04Z, grind_long and abs_veto_long together. The tournament read the new switch file at 14:45:04.329Z and had both buy orders on the wire at 14:45:04.335Z and .343Z — six and fourteen milliseconds later. Four lots, four winners, +$181.50. That is not a lucky fill; that is a decision arriving and a gate acting on it inside the same second.

2. The bench was right on the week's ugliest tape, and I can price it. Thursday's US open whipsawed the other book for −$1,150 in eight minutes. All six gates were off. Replaying the four trades they wanted on the tick tape, at five different stop widths, the bench saved between $21.80 and $364.20 — negative sign at every width, $292.56 at the desk's live 1.0×ATR stop. Sign-stable, so it is a verdict, not a coin flip.

3. The "$205–$705 lateness cost" does not survive the stop sweep. The desk's own router ledger says Friday's arm was 20 minutes late and that the lateness cost 3.3× what the arm made. I re-ran it as a like-for-like one-slot simulation — armed early versus armed when it actually armed, same exit rule both sides — and the delta is −$87.60 at the live stop width and +$82 to +$104 at the other four. The sign flips. By this desk's own rule that is NO VERDICT, and the big number was an upper bound built from counting one trend four times.

4. The Claim button is now the desk's main exit, and it is costing money. 23 of 32 legs closed on MANUAL_CLAIM this week — 71.9%, against 9.8% over the previous three weeks. On the two tournament legs I can price exactly, hand-claiming left −$75.14 on the table: grind_long_A was claimed at +$41.50 and its own 2.5R target printed eight minutes later, worth +$118.60.

5. Nothing stopped out. Not once. Zero STOP exits, zero STOP_UNFILLED, on either book, all week. STOP_UNFILLED is now clean for four consecutive weeks after 22 of them cost −$1,182.50 in week 29. That fix is holding.

Three signals, six legs (every gate runs an A and a B lot — same signal, same stop, different exit; they are a scale-out, not an experiment, so "6 of 6 winners" is really 3 of 3).

⚠ This table is not evidence. Here is exactly why.

You told me on 1 August that win rate is never a kill criterion and that everything gets judged on expectancy and robustness. Applying that honestly to this table kills the table, not the gates. Three signals on one day cannot pass a robustness test because none of the tests can even be run.

  • Leave-one-day-out: there is one day. Remove it and there is nothing. Undefined.
  • Strip-the-best: drop capitulation_long and you have +$181.50 on two signals; drop two and you have +$63.50 on one. It stays positive all the way down, which sounds good and means nothing at n=1.
  • Placebo / shuffle: a shuffle test on three observations has no power whatsoever. Not run — deliberately.
  • Out-of-sample: there is no in-sample to be out of.

Verdict: NOT JUDGED. +$330 is neither a vindication nor a fluke; it is a sample too small to be either. For scale, the tournament's all-time book is 747 legs, −$3,905.00, 40.0% of legs green — this week recovered 8.5% of that hole. I would rather say that plainly now than let "100% win rate" wander into a decision.

3 · Why it only traded once — the week in switch positions

The tournament did not fail to find trades. It was switched off. Two separate mechanisms did that, and they are worth keeping apart in your head because only one of them is a judgement.

(a) The 20 August operator stand-down ran until Wednesday evening. Every router tick from Monday 00:00Z to Wednesday 19:55Z says the same thing: "tournament STOOD DOWN — all six gates OFF and HELD, nothing armed to bench, any 'on' is dropped before it applies." And reactivate_gates confirms it from the other side — at Paris midnight on Monday and Tuesday it logged HELD (not auto-armed): abs_veto_long, abs_veto_short, capitulation_long, exhaustion_short, grind_long, rgv_short. All six. The stand-down lifted at 19:59:32Z on Wednesday and the router picked it up on the very next tick. So Monday and Tuesday's zero is by construction, and you cannot read anything about the gates into it.

(b) From Wednesday night, the roster came back but momentum stayed benched-by-default. reactivate_gates re-armed three gates each night (abs_veto_short, capitulation_long, exhaustion_short) and deliberately start-benched the two momentum gates under the MONDAY #2 rule — "router arms on evidence". The router then benched two of the three within about 35 seconds. So the week's armed time looks like this.

The one meaningfully-armed gate was armed by a cron, not by a decision. capitulation_long got 18.8% of the week because it is the only gate reactivate_gates re-arms that the router chooses not to bench — it is a reversion gate with no start-benched flag, and the router said so at every tick ("capitulation_long stays on through the quiet"). Holding it on was a decision, repeated hundreds of times. Arming it was not. It was awake at 14:00Z on Friday because of a rota, and it made $148.50. Being right by rota is worth having and it is not the same as being right.

Three of the six gates were armed for under an hour each, and one for 103 seconds. exhaustion_short's entire week of permission is three roughly-35-second slivers where reactivate_gates writes on at 22:00:00Z and the router writes off at 22:00:32–38Z. That is two programs disagreeing, not a strategy being tested. It cannot be graded this week and I am not going to pretend it was benched on judgement.

5 · Was the arm 20 minutes late? I re-ran it, and the answer is NO VERDICT

The router ledger's headline for that window is that the arm was 20m17s late and that the lateness cost $205–$705 against +$181.50 banked — a bigger error term than anything on its scoreboard. That is a serious claim and it deserved a serious re-derivation, so I did one from scratch off the raw tape.

Method. I pulled every SUPPRESSED-OPEN line for grind_long_A between 13:00Z and the arm — 789 of them — and collapsed them into distinct impulses with a 30-second gap rule (that reproduces exactly the impulse times the ledger names, so we are looking at the same events). Entry ATR comes from signal_journal at the signal. Each impulse is then replayed on the gate's own live exit — scalp to 2.5R, stop k×ATR — on 5-second MNQ bars, at $2.00 a point and $1.50 the round trip, with the stop swept 0.5× to 1.5×.

The crucial correction: one slot holds one position. Pricing each impulse independently and adding them up counts one trend four times over — it is the same mistake as calling a rolling window "3-of-3 confirmed". So I ran it as a sequential simulation: the slot takes the first opportunity it is allowed, is busy until that trade resolves, then takes the next. Then I ran the identical simulation starting at the moment the router actually armed, and differenced them.

Stop widthArmed 13:40 (early)Armed 14:45 (actual)Early − actualRead
0.50 × ATR+$56.54  (4 trades)−$25.52+$82.06early better
0.75 × ATR+$208.78 (4)+$118.60+$90.18early better
1.00 × ATR (live)+$31.00 (3)+$118.60−$87.60early WORSE
1.25 × ATR+$223.02 (3)+$118.60+$104.42early better
1.50 × ATR+$209.97 (3)+$118.60+$91.37early better

NO VERDICT The sign flips across the sweep, and at the width the desk actually runs it flips the wrong way. Arming an hour earlier would have taken two stop-outs (−$53.72 and −$70.58) before the winner, and left the slot occupied at 14:45 so it would have missed the trade it actually took. This desk's own rule is that a replay is a verdict only if its sign survives the stop-width sweep. This one does not, so the honest answer to "was the arm late?" is we do not know, and the $601 figure is an upper bound built by counting one uptrend four times.

What is not in doubt, and is the useful half: the router's direction read was right both times. Of the nine grind_long impulses in that window, the four before 14:22 all stopped at every width (chop — the bench was correctly saving money) and four of the five after 14:24 reached target at the live width (break — the bench was correctly costing money). Two regimes, opposite signs, and the router flipped between them. That is the thing to keep. What we cannot price is whether flipping ten minutes sooner would have been worth anything, because with one slot and a 1.0×ATR stop, it would not have been.

6 · What the benching actually cost — and why most of it was free

Across the week the five active gates logged 380 distinct blocked impulses (the signal_journal, collapsed on a 2-minute gap). The tempting headline is "380 trades we were not allowed to take". It is wrong, and by a factor of three, because most of those gates could not have fired anyway — their own ATR floor was already refusing them, and suppressed_by='switch_off' only tells you which check ran first, not what would have happened.

So seven out of every ten "blocked" fires this week cost nothing to block, and this is not a small correction — it is the difference between "the router is strangling 380 trades" and "the router made about 117 decisions that could have gone either way". It also lands almost exactly where the same measurement landed before (96.3% this week against 95.8% previously), so it is a structural property of grind_long, not a quirk of this tape: the gate spends nearly all of its life asking for trades it is not allowed to have for a completely different reason.

The practical consequence for you: when someone quotes a benching cost, ask whether the gate carries a floor. Only grind_long and capitulation_long do. For the other four, every blocked impulse is real money one way or the other.

In plain terms: most of what the bench "saved" is really the desk's stop being tight enough to guarantee those trades lost. The router was right that the tape was untradeable as this desk trades it. It is not evidence that the signals were wrong about direction — two of the four were right about direction and were killed by the stop. That is a rehab question, not a routing one, and it belongs to Part 1.5.

Why it matters: a hand-claim measures your timing, not the gate's edge. It truncates the exit stack that arming the gate was supposed to unlock, so the gate gets scored on a number it did not produce — and that cuts both ways, understating good gates and flattering bad ones. So the tournament's booked +$330.00 was worth +$405.14 on the gates' own exits. The other claim (abs_veto_long_B) beat its own target by a point — your timing was genuinely better on that one — which is exactly why this needs measuring rather than asserting in either direction.

The rule to take away, and it is cheap to apply: read exit_reason before you read pnl_usd. Any MANUAL_CLAIM row is scoring you, not the gate. At 4.4% of trades all-time that was a footnote; at 72% of the week it is the main exit mechanism on the desk, and it is concentrated in exactly the hand-watched windows where we do the grading.

It is the right call to keep the fix and stop worrying about it; it would be the wrong call to say it has been stress-tested lately.

10 · The direction-router trial — how it actually behaved

In every one of those holes the switch file simply stops changing, which looks identical to "the router considered it and decided nothing". There is no alert on a missing tick. That is a cheap thing to add and it is the difference between a quiet router and an absent one.

11 · Day-type split — and why I am not giving you one

The section is supposed to answer "did a gate's P&L depend on trend versus chop". It cannot be answered this week and any table that appears to answer it would be fabricated. The tournament traded on one day. There is no second cell to compare against. One day is not a split.

What I can tell you about the week's regime, from the tape rather than from trades:

  • There was no trend day. All five sessions travelled between 9.5 and 11.9 times their own range in RTH before settling. The most directional close was Thursday at +167.5 points on 280 of range, and Thursday is also the whippiest full day of the five. Nothing this week looks like a trend day.
  • The one day with real volatility is the day the gates traded. Friday carried 374.8 points of range and a 1-minute ATR of 19.50, against 212–296 and 12.80–15.83 on the other four.
  • The real split is time-of-day, and it is sharper than anything else I found. Exactly 9 of grind_long's 242 blocked impulses all week cleared its 22.0 ATR floor — and all nine of them, on four separate days, fell between 13:40Z and 14:37Z. Outside that single hour the gate did not clear its own floor once in 120 hours. Whatever grind_long is, it is a US-open instrument and nothing else, and that is worth testing properly with more weeks behind it.
  • So the "split" that actually exists is vol, not direction. The gates fired on the one day vol was high enough to let them, which is what the floors are for. Whether their edge depends on trend versus chop is untested and stays untested.

I would rather hand you a clean "cannot be answered" than a two-row table with n=3 in one cell and n=0 in the other.

P1.5 REHABILITATION — never bench a gate at face value

Garrath — the rule is that nothing gets written off on its P&L alone. If a gate is red, the job is to find out how it could work, and to print the treatments that failed by name so nobody digs the same hole next Friday. Three things were red this week and they are red for three completely different reasons, which is the point: one is a software fault, one is a missing stop, and only one of them is actually a gate. The headline is that the gate everyone would have benched is the one with the least wrong with it, and the loss that looks like bad luck was structural.

1 · First, strip the malfunctions out of the strategy verdict

Two of the week's lots are not trading decisions at all. They have to come out before any gate is judged, and they have to be reported, because a fault that gets quietly absorbed into a gate's P&L is a fault nobody fixes:

2 · REHAB TARGET ONE — abs_veto_short, −$170.00 over 22 lots

This is the only red gate that is actually a gate. It fired 22 lots at 32% win for −$170.00, and the reflex is to bench it. Before that, the treatment.

2.1 — What KIND of loser is it? (the root-cause step)

There are only two kinds of losing trade and they need opposite fixes. A chase never goes green at all — it is adverse from the first tick, and that is an ENTRY problem. A give-back goes green and hands it back, and that is an EXIT problem. Measured inside each trade's own life, on the tick tape:

0 of the 15 losing lots were chases. Not one of them was adverse from the first tick — the worst-behaved loser still got 6 points onside and the median loser reached +11.25 points, which is $21.00 a lot sitting on the screen before it turned round. So the reflex diagnosis is wrong. This is not a gate buying tops; every one of these entries worked, briefly.

The difference between a winner and a loser here is not whether the trade went onside, it is how far: the winners' median peak is +30.25 points against the losers' +11.25. That is a give-back shape, and give-back shapes are an EXIT question — so the exit is where the treatment has to start, which is the opposite of where this desk usually looks.

2.2b — But is that the STOP, or is it the target riding along with it?

The sweep above moves the stop and the target together, because R is defined on risk. That means “tighter is better” could just be “a nearer target gets hit more often”, which is a completely different instruction. Nothing clears the bar. The two that beat the as-traded number do it by cutting winners along with losers, and the stand-down-after-two-stops rule is the “wall of stops” idea. ★ REV2 fixes its count, which the report gave as three here and four on the action card. It is THREE independent populations, and this is the canonical list — every other mention of the rule points here: (1) mechanically on 104 signals last week; (2) live across last week’s tape; (3) abs_veto_short’s 22 lots this week, in the table above. The card said “fourth” by counting the run-state work as a population; it is not one — that work refuted the same principle on a different question and never tested this rule on a sample of its own, so it is supporting reasoning, not evidence. Three is the number. Post it as REFUTED and stop proposing it.

So what IS the treatment for abs_veto_short?

Three things are now closed off. It is NOT a stop-width change — ten cells across two sweeps, every one negative. It is NOT a filter — none keeps the winners. And it is NOT a bench on a knife-edge, because the sign survived, so a bench here would at least be honest.

What the excursion table actually says is that the entries work and then stop working: median peak +30.25 points on the winners against +11.25 on the losers, with nothing adverse from the first tick. The live experiment that addresses exactly that is the 55-second continuation-confirm — it re-requires the burst to PERSIST before entering, which is a filter on the difference between an 11-point poke and a 30-point move. This week its mirrors are the top of the shadow board (+$332 over 46 fires) while the live gate lost $203 over 22. Part 2 is where that promotion is argued, and it is the one real proposal this report makes about this gate.

The honest caveat, stated before Part 2 rather than after it: the shadow mirror does NOT model the live gate's default-veto on thin tape, so it over-fires, and it enters on the 1-minute bar open where the live decider quotes the tick it fired on. Both biases run in the mirror's favour. It is an upper bound, and it is presented as one.

2.4 — ★ REV2: THE EXIT LADDER — the treatment §2.1 diagnosed and §2.2–§2.3 never ran

The dangling diagnosis

§2.1 ends on a sentence that commits this section to something: “that is a give-back shape, and give-back shapes are an EXIT question — so the exit is where the treatment has to start.” What followed was §2.2 sweeping the stop, §2.2b sweeping the stop again, §2.3 sweeping time-of-day and stand-down filters, and a recommendation of the 55-second confirm, which is an entry filter. Not one rung of an exit ladder was ever tested on the gate this report says has an exit-shaped loss. Here they are, on the same 22 lots, with the winners-kept column carried all the way through.

Every lot raced from its own entry on the tick tape, three-hour cap, stop wins a tie. The stop and the target come from the VENUE, not from an ATR estimate — every lot’s protective StopLimitOrder auxPrice is in the tournament journal, so R = |entry − stop| is exact, and the live target model (the atr_split=22 quiet-tape clip: Lot A banks $40, Lot B takes max(1.75×ATR, $60) below a 22-point ATR) is confirmed to the tick. Calibration: 18 of 18 machine-closed lots reproduce their own live exit reason.

★ AND A LOSING RIDER IS STRUCTURALLY SILENT — that is the real defect

The reason this ran for six hours is that nothing was shouting. The rider pages on peak give-back and on stalls; below its arm threshold there is no stop, no trail and no alert, so a position that is simply losing produces no output at all. Both of the tools you would naturally check print “flat, $0” while it happens, because the trade has not CLOSED yet and they count closed rows.

The rehabilitation of the rider is not an entry change and it is not a threshold change. It is a stop. A 3.0×ATR protective stop on the rider's own book, sized off its entry ATR, is the single highest-value change on this week's card — and ★ REV2 corrects both halves of what Rev1 said here: not 1.5×, and not “$1,000 on one day” but +$462 on the week’s closed book. It is also the change that removes the report’s headline: every width tested, including 3.0×, closes Friday’s 13:13Z entry by 13:31:55Z — six and a half hours before the gateway wedged.

1.6 THE DAY RIDER — the weekly performance review

Garrath — the rider lost −$1,576.94 this week across 13 entries and 26 legs, against the six-gate tournament’s +$330.00 on three signals. That is the first losing week the rider has had since it started keeping a ledger, and I want to be straight about where the money went before anything else: −$2,149.44 of it is a single position opened on Friday 21 August that never got flattened, and a further $734.50 is fifteen fills that printed at prices the tape never traded at. Strip the carry-in and the week is +$572.50. Strip the bad fills as well and it is +$1,175.00. Neither of those two items is the strategy. What is the strategy had a mixed week and one genuinely bad afternoon, and the four questions you set get four clean answers below. The short version: the entries were fine when they were the rider’s own and poor when they were not, the thresholds are on a plateau and there is nothing to change this week, your hand was the best exit on the book by a mile, and the weak day is Thursday — a rich tape we converted 0.7% of.

★★ If you read nothing else — six things, in order

1. The rider stopped being an automatic strategy this week and became a manual terminal. The drift detector got to place exactly two of the week’s thirteen entries. The other eleven were your BUY/SELL presses. On Monday, Thursday and Friday the automatic path never even ran — a position was already open, the once-per-session latch was set, and the rider spent the whole 13:30–15:00 window printing “already traded this session — no re-entry”.

2. The validated entry window is doing real work. Four entries landed inside 13:38–14:09 and made +$1,288.00. The other nine lost −$2,864.94 (−$715.50 without the carry-in). All four entries that never showed a single point of profit after boarding were outside the window.

3. Nothing to change on the thresholds, and I can now say that with 49 sessions behind it. The two live fires cleared their floors by +0.240/+0.067 and +0.094/+0.057 — no scrapes. Across the whole 49-session sample the median ER margin is +0.251 and the median RT margin +0.122. Only six sessions ever came within +0.02 of a floor, and those six are worth +$1,470 on the live exit — raising the floor would have thrown away four winners worth +$3,094 to dodge two losers worth −$1,624.

4. Your claims were worth +$5,426.50 this week. Every lot you claimed by hand, held instead to the 20:40 clock, would have finished at −$5,614.50. You closed the same lots for −$188.00. That is not the rider’s design working; that is you overriding the rider’s design, and this week it was right.

5. Fifteen fills were off-tape and every single one was against us. 15 of the week’s 63 executions printed outside the high/low of the tape in a ±30-second window, all adverse, every one of them the residual leg of a split order priced at the on-tape leg × (1 ± 0.001). Fifteen for fifteen in the same direction. Cost: $734.50, which is 47% of the week’s reported loss.

6. Thursday is the weak day and it is a strategy fault, not a tape fault. Six entries, twelve legs, +$16.50 banked out of $2,478.00 of available favourable excursion — a 0.7% capture on a tape that offered a 283-point range and a clean +179-point up-move. Two entries at 13:34 and 13:35 — a buy, a panic-out 38 seconds later, and a flip short into the low — cost −$1,150.00 in seven minutes.

0 · How I measured, and the one instrument I had to rebuild CALIBRATED

Everything below is re-derived from the 5-second tape, not inherited. Two things had to be fixed before any number was trustworthy.

The live detector runs at :06 past the minute now, not :21. The tick offset moved around 17 August. I calibrated the replay against the rider’s own leaning field rather than guessing it: the live service ticks at HH:MM:06 and the newest 5-second bar in capture.db at that instant is the one starting at HH:MM:00. With that cutoff the replay reproduces the two live reads exactly — and it is a sharp test, because the read five seconds either side does not confirm at all:

⚠ And scripts/day_rider_lab.py is reading the wrong bars. Its minute_bars() query is SELECT … FROM bars WHERE symbol='MNQ' with no timeframe filter, and the lake holds seven timeframes for MNQ. Inside the 13:30–20:40 window alone that is 31,500 non-5s rows — 11.0% of everything it reads (17,881 1min, 7,484 1m, 2,498 3m, 1,827 5mins, 1,520 5m, 290 1hour). An hourly bar’s high and low collapse into a single minute bucket, which inflates that minute’s range and true range. Efficiency is |net| / path and roundtrip is |net| / range, so both get moved. Every number in this section uses timeframe='5s' only, aggregated the way drift._minute_bars does it. This is a one-line fix and it belongs on Saturday’s list.

The window is earning its keep — and here is the sharpest version of it

Four entries inside 13:38–14:09: +$1,288.00. Nine outside: −$2,864.94 (−$715.50 if you set the carry-in aside). And look at the MFE column: four entries never showed a single point of profit after boarding — 21 Aug 13:13, 27 Aug 13:34, 27 Aug 13:35 and 27 Aug 16:58. All four were outside the window. Between them they lost −$3,508.44. That is n=4 in one week, so it is not a law — but it is exactly the shape the validated window was drawn around, and it repeated four times in five days.

Do we board too late? This is the question the “detection latency” work raised, and on the rider’s own instrument the answer is no. Across all 49 sessions in the lake with a full 13:30–20:40 5-second tape, the detector confirms at a median of +9 minutes (IQR +8 to +13, worst +41), 48 of 49 inside 13:38–14:09, with a median of 95 points already travelled and 155 points still to come. So we board with roughly 38% of the eventual swing gone and 62% still available. And how far it has already run tells you almost nothing about what is left: Spearman +0.109 against remaining MFE and −0.079 against money. Boarding late is not this strategy’s problem.

⚠ But the automatic path only got to run twice in five days

The rider carries a once-per-session entered latch. Any position — automatic or a manual press — consumes the slot for the whole day. This week it fired on three of five sessions: Monday it was the carried-over Friday long, Thursday the 07:20 buy, Friday the 12:39 buy. On each of those days the 13:30–15:00 window printed nothing but “already traded this session — no re-entry”. So I replayed what the detector would have done had it been free:

The latch saved money this week — between $1,476 and $3,546 of it. That is one week and I am not building a policy on it. The point is the opposite one: the desk currently has no way to tell the difference between “the rider declined to trade” and “the rider was never asked”, and for three of five sessions this week it was the second. If we keep both books on one latch we should at least log the detector’s read on the days it is muzzled, so this table can be built from the journal instead of from a replay.

Roundtrip was the constraint the whole way: at 13:38 efficiency was already clear at 0.195 but roundtrip was 0.287. And at five-second resolution it is sharper still: on Tuesday the read at 13:38:01 confirms at 0.390/0.517 and the read at 13:38:06, five seconds later, does not (0.314/0.440). The entry is a genuine coin-toss on a five-second boundary, which is the strongest argument I have seen for the dwell/confirmation idea — and also the reason a single late snapshot mis-scores this strategy so badly.

⚠ One prior finding does not reproduce, and I think I know why

An earlier day-rider study recommended raising the efficiency floor from 0.15 to 0.25 (38 sessions, 15 June–7 August). On my 49 sessions that lift is real only if you price it on hold-to-the-clock — $8,580 → $14,296. On the armed trail, which is what the desk actually runs, it goes the other way: $22,102 → $20,510. The samples overlap but are not the same window, so this is not a refutation. It is a warning that the recommendation was measured on a policy the desk does not run, and it should not be actioned until it is re-tested on the live exit. PARKED — revive if the 0.25 floor beats 0.15 on the armed trail across a 60+ session sample.

4 · WHICH EXIT CAPTURED IT? THE HAND WON

Capture is the leg’s realised dollars over the best that leg could have made between the entry and its own close, in dollars at $2.00/point on its own lot count, net of $1.50/RT on both sides. A leg that never went into profit contributes zero to “available”, so the denominator is never flattered by a losing entry.

Two things jump out. The target ladder is doing precise work at its bottom two rungs and nothing at its top two. Five lots came off on TARGET_100 / TARGET_200 for +$633.50 at 86–92% capture, five for five green. The $400 and $600 rungs did not fire once all week — no lot was ever 200 points onside on a 4-lot entry. And the trail armed once in five sessions. That is not a defect, it is arithmetic: the arm bar is 4×ATR frozen at entry, ATR was 28.8–41.2 this week, so the bar sat at +115 to +165 points and only one entry ever got there. Across the 49-session sample it arms on 28 of 49 (57%), median 4×ATR = 161 points against a median MFE of 155. It is a coin-flip by construction, and it is the design you settled on.

6 · The three faults that cost real money ACTION

(a) The carry-in — a gateway outage that arrived 42 minutes early. On Friday 21 August the rider was long 4 lots from 13:13Z. The hard flat is 20:40Z. The watchdog log shows the IB gateway went unreachable at 19:58:50Z and stayed unreachable until 23:44:50Z — 3h46m, 114 consecutive SKIP venue read failed polls, straddling the flatten clock completely. The position rode the weekend and you closed it by hand on Monday at 11:59Z.

Exit that was supposed to happenPricePointsP&L on 4 lots
Fri 20:40Z — the hard flat29,381.25−110.7−$891.44
Fri 20:58Z — last print before the halt29,374.25−117.7−$947.44
Mon 11:59Z — what actually happened29,224.00−244.7−$2,149.44
Cost of the failed flatten——−$1,258.00

The excursion tells you how bad it could have been: MFE −3.4 points — the position was never once in profit — and MAE −375.2 points, or −$3,002 on 4 lots, hit while the market was open and nobody was watching. And the outage is not a freak: the same blackout starts at 20:40:50Z on 17 Aug, 20:42:50Z on 27 Aug, 20:06:50Z on 23 Aug. Two of those begin within three minutes of the 20:40 flat. The desk’s hard-flat clock is sitting on the exact edge of a recurring gateway blackout with zero margin, and the only reason 21 August is the one that hurt is that the outage happened to arrive 42 minutes early. The watchdog, meanwhile, printed “ok position 4.0 managed” 1,908 times while that position was open, because the heartbeat was fresh — a strategy that is running and a strategy that can reach the venue are not the same thing.

(b) Fifteen off-tape fills, all against us, $734.50. I checked every one of the week’s 63 executions for containment inside the tape’s high/low in a ±30-second window. 15 failed. Every single one is the residual leg of a split order, and every single one prices at the on-tape leg × (1 ± 0.001) in the adverse direction:

Fifteen for fifteen in the same direction is not slippage; on a fair coin that is a 1-in-33,000 event. The worst single one is 28.75 points. The Wednesday automatic entry is the one that stings — 3 of its 4 lots filled 17 points above the highest print in the surrounding half-minute, which turned a $19.00 day into what should have been $121.00. Every capture percentage in §4 is therefore slightly pessimistic, and every entry price in the trade table is contaminated on those 18 lots. This is a known, recurring pattern on this desk and it is now large enough to be a line item.

(c) The rider goes blind on its own positions outside 13:30–21:00Z. Two of the week’s manual entries were opened outside the US session. For the Thursday 07:20 entry the rider held 4 lots for 371 minutes with ahead_pt pinned at 0.0 for 370 of them, peak frozen at the entry price, trail never set, arm_atr = 0.0, and the note falling back to “trail not armed (need +150 [fixed])” because it had no ATR to scale with. Same on Friday’s 12:39 entry for 50 of its 65 minutes. The drift read is gated to 13:30–21:00Z and the manage path is downstream of it, so a position opened before the open is carried, not managed — no peak, no trail, no give-back, no exit at all except your hand. Both of those trades made money (+$377.50 and +$187.00), which is exactly why it is worth flagging now rather than after one goes the other way.

So what do I actually do?

Nothing to the strategy. The thresholds are on a plateau, the window is validated and holding, the exits behaved the way they are designed to behave, and the one week of adverse evidence is not enough to move any of them. That is the honest answer and I would rather write it than invent a tweak.

Three things to the plumbing, in priority order. (1) Move the first flatten attempt earlier than 20:40 and page before the attempt, not after it — that is the $1,258 item and it will recur. (2) Assert tape-containment per execution at book time — that is $734.50 this week alone and it is mechanically detectable. (3) Fix the timeframe filter in day_rider_lab.py before the next report reuses it.

One thing to the logging. Record the drift read on days the rider is muzzled by the latch. It cost nothing, and it is the difference between knowing this strategy’s hit rate and guessing at it.

P2 THE SHADOW DESK & PROMOTION — what earned a live slot, and what the open rider actually needs

Garrath — the short version before the detail. One thing on the shadow board is ready and it is ready two-sided: abs_veto_55s is $5,302.50 over 433 tick-repriced trades, it is green in all seven ISO weeks it has existed, it is still $3,899.00 after you delete its ten best trades, and both directions earn — LONG $1,691.00 and SHORT $3,611.50. Nothing else on the board clears that bar. The open rider is the week's big piece of work and the answer is not the one you asked for — it is better. You said we need to detect a juicy day and block the rider when conditions are not juicy. I built the pre-session day classifier, swept it properly and it died: the best rule looks brilliant on its own (p = 0.5%) and then evaporates the moment you charge it for the 220 rules I tried to find it (family-wise p = 29%), and every top rule loses money out-of-sample. But a second, causal idea passed everything: stop each rider arm for the day the first time it changes direction. That single rule takes the open rider from −$1,835.00 to +$1,244.50 over the same 15 days and 119 trades, it survives leave-one-day-out, strip-the-best-3, both cadences, both stop widths and the gated twins it was never fitted on, and its family-wise placebo is 0.3%. It is not day detection. It is day abandonment, decided from inside the session on information the rider already has. And on the exit lab I have to give you a flat no on the headline rung: BIG-TREND does not exist. On 68,600 minutes of extended tape, ER ≥ 0.50 occupies 3.00% of the clock in 544 episodes whose median length is two minutes. You cannot build a "ride the big trend" exit for a state that is over before the trade is.

The five things that survived the skeptic this week
  1. abs_veto_55s, TWO-SIDED — PROMOTE. $5,302.50 / 433 / 48.0% win / +$12.25 a trade. Green in 7 of 7 weeks. Strip its best ten trades and it is still +$3,899.00.
  2. The 55s veto's own evidence is the cleanest number on the desk. On the same raw thrust entries, the ones it refuses lose −$5,287.00 at 22.3% win; the ones it keeps make +$5,239.00 at 49.0% win. It splits a break-even book into two halves that are almost mirror images.
  3. ONE-DIRECTION-PER-DAY on the open rider. −$1,835.00 → +$1,244.50 over 15 days. Family-wise placebo p = 0.3%. Helps 13 of 15 days, both cadences, both stops, and the drift-gated twins.
  4. The pre-session day classifier is REFUTED as built — and that is a survivor, because it stops us shipping a rule that only looks good because I tried 220 of them.
  5. The exit ladder has exactly one proven rung: grind MED-TREND at Lot A 0.75R / Lot B 1.0R, +$7.70 a signal on n=215, and it sits in a real parameter plateau rather than on a spike. Every other cell of the ladder failed strip-the-best-3.

2 · THE PROMOTION — abs_veto_55s, and promote it two-sided

This is thrust_loose plus a 55-second continuation confirm: the gate sees a thrust, waits 55 seconds, and only takes it if the burst is still going rather than being absorbed. Here is the full battery from scripts/abs_veto_robustness.py, run tonight on the completed week.

4 · ★★★ THE OPEN RIDER — you were right about both halves, and the fix is not the one we went looking for

Your words, and they set the whole section: "open rider best shadow again … but i know they bleed on other days. thats where im saying we need detection some how to block open rider if conditions arent juicy."

The open rider (odr_*) is the simplest thing on the board and that is what makes it such a good test bed. There is no gate and no signal. Between 13:00 and 14:45 UTC, every N minutes, it looks at the last 15 minutes of tape and goes with the sign of it. Target is 2R, coupled to the stop. Eight arms run forward: four ungated (sims 54–57, cadence 5 or 10 minutes × stop 2.0 or 3.0 ×ATR) and four drift-gated twins (sims 60–63) that differ in exactly one bit — a direction gate that refuses an entry disagreeing with the confirmed drift.

4.1 — First, the numbers have moved a long way since the lead was written

The lead I was handed described five days, 08-10 to 08-14: two green days paying $1,748 against three red days losing $2,229. There are now fifteen days, and the picture is much worse. The 2.0×ATR arms stopped after 08-14, so the only arms with a full fifteen-day history are the two 3.0×ATR ungated cells — that pair is the open rider book from here on, and every number below is theirs unless I say otherwise.

Both halves of what you said are confirmed, and then some. Seven green days paid $2,500.00. Eight red days lost −$4,335.00. The average — −$15.42 a trade — describes not one single day the thing actually had. And the oracle that cheats by knowing the labels in advance is +$2,500.00 over three weeks = $833 a week, which does clear your "few hundred a week" bar. So the prize is real and the problem genuinely is day selection. But note what has happened to the oracle since the lead was written: on five days it was $1,748 a week; on fifteen days it is $833 a week, because the two monster green days have not been repeated at that size. The prize is shrinking as the sample grows, which is the normal fate of a number computed on five days.

4.2 — The pre-session day classifier, built properly — and it FAILS

The rider's first entry is at 13:00 UTC, which is half an hour before the US cash open. So a genuinely causal day classifier can only use the overnight and pre-open tape up to 13:00. I built eleven such features per day from the 5-second parquet lake — overnight range and net drift, ATR-14 on 5-minute bars and that ATR relative to its own trailing 10-session median, efficiency over the last 60 and 180 minutes, the last-3-hours range absolute and relative, volume-expansion ratio, and relative volume — and swept every single-feature threshold rule in both directions that keeps between 3 and 12 of the 15 days. That is a family of 220 rules.

Here are the best of them, each with the naive placebo you would normally quote: skip the same number of days at random, 4,000 times, and see where the rule lands.

rule (all causal, all knowable at 13:00 UTC)days kepttradesnet$/trgreen days keptnaive placebo p
last-3h range ≤ 0.50× its trailing norm325$1,829.50+$73.183 / 30.5%
overnight net drift ≥ +49.25 pt756$1,646.00+$29.395 / 70.8%
ER-60 ≤ 0.074 (a calm pre-open)540$1,641.50+$41.044 / 51.2%
ER-180 ≤ 0.055541$1,338.00+$32.634 / 53.0%
ATR-14 (5m) ≥ 26.0 pt645$984.00+$21.874 / 66.0%
(mirror) last-3h range ≥ 0.587× norm1294−$3,664.50−$38.984 / 1299.6%

Read that table cold and you would ship the first row tomorrow: a rule that keeps three days, catches all three greens, makes $1,829.50 and has a 0.5% placebo. It is a mirage, and here is the test that proves it.

The family-wise placebo — the test that killed the day classifier

A 0.5% p-value means "one rule in two hundred would do this by luck". I tried two hundred and twenty rules. So the right question is not "could this rule happen by chance", it is "could the best of 220 rules happen by chance". I answered it directly: shuffle which day's P&L belongs to which day's features, re-run the entire 220-rule sweep, take the winner, and repeat 2,000 times.

whatbest-rule net
the real best rule$1,829.50
shuffled data, median best rule$1,623.00
shuffled, 90th percentile$2,246.00
shuffled, 95th percentile$2,337.00
family-wise p29.0%

Random noise, mined the same way, beats our best rule three times in ten. The 0.5% was entirely an artefact of not charging myself for the search. There is no pre-session day classifier here.

And the out-of-sample leg buries it. Fit on the first ten days (08-10 to 08-21), test on this week (08-24 to 08-28):

rule fitted on the first 10 daysin-sample netdays kept OOSOOS netwhat trading ALL 5 days would have done
overnight net ≥ +49.25$2,150.001−$504.00−$2,350.00
overnight net ≥ +62.75$2,084.001−$504.00−$2,350.00
relative volume ≤ 0.862$1,895.502−$1,365.00−$2,350.00
last-3h range ≤ 87 pt$1,829.501−$861.00−$2,350.00

Every one of them loses money out-of-sample, and the apparent improvement over the −$2,350.00 all-days figure is just arithmetic — the week averaged −$470 a day, so keeping one day and losing $504 is exactly the random expectation, and keeping two and losing $1,365 is worse than random. The rules did not pick days; they picked fewer days.

⚠ And the power limit, stated plainly. Fifteen days cannot separate a real day classifier from noise. What the family-wise test tells us is not "there is no juicy-day signal in the tape" — it is "with 15 days and 11 features I cannot tell one from luck, and neither can anyone else." PARKED, not refuted. Reviving it needs roughly 40–50 rider days with a feature set fixed in advance so the search is one rule, not 220. That is about ten more weeks of forward shadow. It is free, so we should keep collecting.

4.3 — ★★ What DID pass: stop the arm for the day the first time it changes direction

While the pre-session work was failing, the per-day table above was saying something out loud. Look at the two best days: 08-13 was seven LONGs and nothing else, and 08-21 was eight SHORTs out of nine. Now look at the bleeders: 08-27 was four longs and six shorts, 08-25 was four and four, 08-18 was four and four. The rider does not lose on "un-juicy" days. It loses on days where it takes both sides. That is a whipsaw signature, and it is knowable during the session without predicting anything.

So the rule is: each arm keeps trading until the first time its side flips; after that it is done for the day. No parameters, no thresholds, no fitting. Causal by construction — every decision uses only trades that have already opened.

The flip anatomy, so you can picture what it actually does. Across the 30 arm-days there is at least one side change on 26 of them (87%), and in 20 of those 26 the very first flip is at the second entry of the day. So most days this rule means "take one or two rides and go home"; on the four no-flip days it means "run the whole session". The average kept day is 2.5 entries against a baseline of 4.0.

4.5 — The 51-day replay, and why it makes me hold this at SHADOW rather than ship it

The rider is fully deterministic — a clock and a sign — so it can be replayed over every day of tape we hold. I re-ran scripts/odr_day_classifier.py tonight over 51 sessions, 2026-06-19 to 2026-08-28, producing 937 replayed trades. That is a 3.4× extension of the sample and it says two uncomfortable things.

First: the replay is not a faithful mirror, so it cannot settle a P&L question. Matched against the real forward shadow book, day for day and cell for cell:

celldaysREAL n / netREPLAY n / netentry timestamps that match exactly

The grand totals are close — −$2,559.50 against −$2,271.75 — but that is luck at the aggregate. Per cell it is badly wrong: odr_c5_s30 is −$1,388.50 in real life and −$335.00 in the replay, a factor of four, and only 59% of its entries even happen at the same second. Use this replay for mechanism questions, never for a dollar verdict.

Second: the replay's headline is a window artefact, and it is a big one. The full 51-day replay comes to +$15,747, which looks like a licence to print money until you ask when the money was made:

windowdaysreplay nreplay netgreen dayswhat was happening

2026-08-10 → 08-2815276−$4,160.395 / 15the rider actually running forward

Every dollar of the +$15,747 and then some sits in a 17-day window when the rider was not trading. The moment it went forward it turned negative. That is the textbook shape of a strategy that was chosen because a backtest window flattered it, and it is the single strongest reason nothing here gets promoted this week.

And now the awkward bit for my own finding. Run the flip rule on all 51 replayed days and it does not help overall:

window (replay)baselinewith the flip ruledelta

2026-07-16 → 08-07$18,504.75$11,329.04−$7,175.71

all 51 days$15,747.07$11,336.50−$4,410.57 · placebo p = 22%
The honest reading, and it is not the flattering one

On the real forward book the flip rule is strong — family-wise p = 0.3%, every subgroup improved, both external checks passed. On the 51-day replay it is negative overall and its entire benefit is concentrated in the same 15 days I found it on. Two readings fit:

  1. The rule is regime-conditional. It fixes a whipsaw that has only been present since early August; on the trending June–July tape, re-entering after a flip was correct.
  2. The rule is fitted to 15 days and the replay is telling me so.

I cannot separate those with the data I have, and the replay is a 74%-faithful mirror so it does not get a casting vote. Verdict: SHADOW, not deploy. The way to settle it costs nothing: add two flip-locked arms (odr_c5_s30_f, odr_c10_s30_f) alongside the existing eight, paired so the only difference is the lock, and let them run. If the lock is real it will show up as a widening gap against its own twin within about a month; if it was fitted, the gap will close. That is a one-bit change to the shadow slate and it is the single highest-value thing on the Saturday card.

4.6 — The drift gate has finally bitten, and it is costing money

The lead said the drift-gated arms (60–63) covered one day and had never rejected an entry. That is out of date — they now cover eleven days and the gate has fired. Paired strictly on days where both twins ran:

pairdaysungated n / netgated n / netdeltaentries the gate blocked$ on the blocked entries

Six blocked entries in eleven days, and all six were winners. The gate has cost $301.00 so far. But six entries decides nothing — that is a coin landing heads six times, and I would say the same if it had saved $301. Note also that blocking an entry frees the slot, so the gated arm sometimes takes a different trade later; that is why the two arms can have the same n and different money. Report it, do not act on it. What would settle it is roughly 40 blocked entries, which at the current rate is about four months. If we want that answer sooner the gate needs to be made more selective, not the arms run longer.

⚠ Never compare gated against ungated on all-time totals. The gated arms started on 08-14 and the ungated on 08-10, so an all-time comparison measures the calendar, not the gate. Every number in the table above is on the 11 shared days only.

Wider wins on 4 of the 5 shared days and the direction of the effect holds. But look at the third row: the wider stop that "won" the A/B has since lost $1,835 over fifteen days. 4.8 — Could ONE day classifier serve both the rider and the gold run-catcher? No.

You flagged that the same shape turned up twice this month — the MNQ rider lives on a few days, and the MGC run-catcher does too (docs/MGC_LEADS_2026-08-14.md: boarded runs +$99.23 over 14, everything else −$373.83 over 35). If the juicy days coincided, one detector would serve two desks and be worth more than either. I tested it directly on the 26 days where we hold both tapes, pricing gold at $10.00 a point.

testresultread
days where "MNQ rider green" agrees with "MGC run-day"12 / 26 = 46%chance agreement given the two base rates is 50%
lift over chance−4 pointsthe agreement is below random
Spearman(rider day $, MGC run $)−0.047nothing
Spearman(rider day $, MGC day ER)−0.119nothing
MNQ's own pre-13:00 features vs MGC run sizeATR +0.003 · ER +0.041 · roundtrip −0.060nothing, three ways

I checked the same question on the real forward book rather than the replay as a sanity pass and got the same answer: 3 of the rider's 7 green days were MGC run-days and 4 of its 8 red days were too. REFUTED — the two instruments' good days are independent. The named test is the coincidence table plus three Spearman correlations at zero, over 26 days. This is worth knowing because it means two detectors, and it means gold's filter problem has to be solved on gold's own tape. The one caveat: "juicy" is defined here as a green rider day and a $300+ gold excursion; a different definition of the shared state (say, a global risk regime) is untested, and that is the one stone left unturned on this question.

The script ships a recon_pure column — it reconstructs what the LIVE pure-6.0 rule would have done, so you can check the reconstruction against what actually happened before you trust the shadow arm. That cross-check has blown out.

Three of those four exited MANUAL_CLAIM — you took the money by hand, and no reconstruction of an automatic rule can reproduce that. So the shadow-vs-live delta of −$366.50 is not interpretable: it is mostly the repricer failing to model your own claims.

What IS still readable is the clip count, because a clip is defined on rMFE and on the shadow arm's own exit, not on the live P&L. Zero clips, three runners, five weeks.

The verdict logic cannot fire either way this week, and the reason is volume, not the rule. grind_long has taken 64 lots on six days since the deploy and exactly two lots this week (both on 08-28, both MANUAL_CLAIM, +$63.50 together). We have not had a genuine trend week for the watch to observe. The two-ratchet stays dead by default and the watch stays open — that is the same call as last week, made for a new reason: last week it was "no clip fired", this week it is "there was almost nothing to fire on, and the repricer is broken enough that I would not trust a clip if one had".

Fix on the Saturday card: the reconstruction needs to skip or separately bucket MANUAL_CLAIM exits rather than pretending the automatic rule produced them. Until it does, the xcheck line is the only honest headline this tool has.

7.1 — Grading the LIVE exhaustion_short fade-scalp trial on actual fills — and a tooling fault that changes the answer

First, a defect I found while doing this, because it invalidates the number the tool prints. scripts/exhaustion_trial_grade.py labels everything from 2026-07-31 onward as "TRIAL A0.5/B1.5" and reports it as a single config: n=94, −$314.50. But the exit config changed underneath it twice. The tracked history of data/exit_overrides.json says exhaustion_short ran a_r 0.75 / b "tight" until 2026-08-16 08:34 UTC, when it was moved to a_r 2.0 / b 2.0 / stop_k 1.5 — a completely different exit with a 50% wider stop. The tool has been stitching two configs together and grading them as one. Split at the real boundary:

The verdict on the fade-scalp trial is worse than the tool said, and cleaner. The trial as actually configured lost −$480.00 over 80 lots at 41% win, and 59% of its exits were stops against 44% before it. A 0.75R first target with a 1.0×ATR stop is asking to be right 60% of the time to break even and it was right 41% of the time. That is a losing bet on this gate and the desk was right to move off it on 08-16.

The current config cannot be graded and I will not pretend otherwise. Fourteen lots, two days, and seven of the fourteen exits are MANUAL_CLAIM — which measures your timing, not the gate's exit stack. And the gate has taken zero live trades this week. There is no fresh live evidence at all; +$165.50 is a two-day anecdote with half its exits taken by hand.

So the honest read has to come from the reprice, which replays every exhaustion entry we hold — 1,063 of them (112 live + 951 shadow), 1,062 of which get a rung label — on the forward 5-second path under both configs:

Two readings of that table before we go on. First, the thrust/absveto rows are built from raw thrust entries (thrust_loose and thrust_short_raw) — the un-vetoed population. 7.3 — ★ Why the BIG-TREND rung will never have n: the regime barely exists

The BIG-TREND rung has been "too thin to deploy from" in every report that has looked at it, and the standing assumption has been that we needed more tape. We now have all the tape and it is still thin, so I measured the rung itself rather than the trades in it. Every minute of the extended tape, classified by the same ER-30 bands the ladder uses:

rungminutes% of the clock
BIG-TREND — ER-30 ≥ 0.502,0603.00%
MED-TREND — 0.30 – 0.5011,78017.17%
STAY-OUT — ER < 0.30 and ATR ≥ 226,6749.73%
SCALP-CHOP — ER < 0.30 and ATR < 2248,08670.10%
total usable minutes68,60055 sessions

And the killer statistic is not the 3% — it is the duration. Those 2,060 minutes are not a handful of long trends. They are 544 separate episodes with a median length of TWO MINUTES and a 90th percentile of nine. The longest continuous BIG-TREND stretch in 2½ months of MNQ tape is 31 minutes.

I checked whether that is an artefact of measuring efficiency over 30 minutes. It is not — slowing the measurement makes the state rarer, not longer:

The verdict on the BIG-TREND rung

REFUTED as an exit rung keyed on ER, and the named tests are these two: (1) the extended sweep — every family's best BIG-TREND cell fails strip-the-best-3, on the widest tape we hold plus a separate desk's out-of-sample pool; and (2) the occupancy measurement above — the state occupies 3% of the clock in two-minute bursts, so a trade that is in BIG-TREND when it opens is almost never in BIG-TREND when it closes. You cannot ride a trend that is over before the trade is.

What would revive it — and this is the actionable part. Do not go looking for more tape; there is none to find and more of it would not help. Redefine the rung on something that persists: a range-break-and-hold state, an ADX-style directional measure, a higher-timeframe structure, or simply "the day's net move is already > 2×ATR and price is on the correct side of VWAP". If a redefined BIG-TREND state lasts 45 minutes instead of 2, the rung becomes measurable and this whole lab can be re-run against it. That is a well-defined piece of work and it is worth a Saturday.

While ranking the board I checked the paired arms against each other row by row, and two pairs are byte-identical on every field — entry timestamp, side, entry price, exit timestamp, exit price, exit reason and repriced P&L:

A perfectly null A/B and a broken A/B look exactly the same on a scoreboard, and these two have been sitting on the board reporting "no difference" for 13 and 13 days respectively. Both are consuming a slate slot and producing nothing. Neither result can be quoted. The range-break stand-down and the 90-second flip timeout are both untested, not "tested and null" — the treatment arm never diverged from the control, which means either the condition never fired or the flag is not wired through to the exit path.

Saturday card: add an assertion to the slate builder that any declared A/B pair whose rows are 100% identical after 20 trades raises a WARN into exec_health. This is the second week running that a paired arm has silently recorded the control's trades under a second name.

  1. Promote abs_veto_55s two-sided on Monday. It is the only thing on the board that survives every test we own, and the long side — the one everybody's instinct says to drop — is worth +$7.98 a trade once the veto is on it.
  2. Add two flip-locked open-rider arms (odr_c5_s30_f, odr_c10_s30_f), paired against their existing twins so the lock is the only difference. One-bit change, zero risk, and it settles the week's best idea in about a month. Do not turn the flip lock on anywhere live — the 51-day replay does not back it outside the window I found it in.
  3. Take the 2R-partial on grind, on the mechanism, and stop quoting its number.
  4. Deploy the grind MED-TREND exit branch banded to ER-30 in [0.30, 0.50), leaving every other rung alone, with rung_grindA_med_live continuing as the referee.
  5. Fix three measurement faults before next Friday: the two-ratchet repricer must bucket MANUAL_CLAIM separately; exhaustion_trial_grade.py must read the config eras out of the git history of exit_overrides.json instead of assuming one boundary; and the slate builder must WARN on byte-identical A/B pairs.
  6. Redefine BIG-TREND on a state that lasts longer than two minutes, then re-run the exit lab against it. Until that happens, every "ride the big trend" result on this desk is being computed on a regime that is over before the trade is.
The three honest limits on everything above
  1. The shadow board over-trades and the paper desk judges. These sims nominate; they place no orders, pay no slippage beyond the tick reprice, and never compete for a slot with each other. abs_veto_55s at 433 trades in seven weeks is roughly ten times the live tournament's rate. Expect the live version to be smaller and slower than the shadow number.
  2. One week, and a quiet one. The live tournament took six trades between Monday and Friday. Almost every conclusion here rests on shadow n, not live n, and grind_long, exhaustion_short and the rgv family took essentially nothing live this week.
  3. No odr arm may be promoted from this report. Every one of the eight is flagged n<40 for a forward A/B claim, the whole family is −$1,835.00 over its 15 days, and its 51-day replay makes all its money in a window when it was not trading. The flip rule is a finding about the rider, not a licence to run it.

P2.5 MID-WEEK MUSINGS — the fresh leads, and gold gets its own chapter

Garrath — lead with what survived, because two things did and both are worth money. First, the standing grind question finally has an answer, and it is none of the three options you asked me to choose between. Grind's losses are not chop-churn to be filtered with efficiency and they are not a trend-day permission problem: on 159 replayed fires the gate's entire bleed is a REGIME and a CLOCK — benching it in ordinary chop and on clean trends turns +$922 into +$2,310, and benching it in the 13:00Z US-open hour alone turns it into +$2,540. Both survive stripping their best three trades and both survive leave-one-day-out, which nothing in this family has ever done before. Second, gold's big finding held up under a much harder test than the one that found it. The claim that gold's runs are grinds and that the exit was the cap, not the filter re-derives on 32 contiguous days with spread-honest fills: the same 165 entries make −$913 on a momentum trail and +$2,702 on a wide stop held long, and the mirror and random-entry controls are deeply negative at every single cell, so the entry is real and the exit really was the ceiling.

And lead with the honest half too, because it is bigger. Gold's most promising shape — the MGC day rider, the 15-cell plateau — is dead. The plateau replicates perfectly inside its own window and then dies on 185 out-of-sample sessions that were sitting in the lake the whole time: direction holds 78–85% on the 26 days we looked at and 49–54% on the 185 we had not, and 0 of 15 cells is positive. The coil bouncer and the London-open fade go the same way for named reasons. The close of the 08-14 gold session was "the missing ingredient is DAYS, not configurations." The days arrived on 2026-08-19 in a backfill nobody announced. They say no.

Read these five flags before any number below

(1) The tournament barely traded, so almost nothing here is this week's realised book. Six tournament trades all week, all on Friday 08-28, all winners, +$330.00 — the stand-down ran Monday and Tuesday and was lifted on the 26th. Every grind number below is therefore a replay: the real gate_grind firing on real bars, with the deployed ATR≥22 floor applied first, exits repriced tick-by-tick as the live two-lot A/B slate (Lot A 2.5R scalp on a 1.0×ATR stop, Lot B the loose-then-lock chandelier), $1.50 per round trip per lot, one position at a time, 180-minute cap, entry on the first tick after the signal bar closes. It is what the deployed configuration would have done across all the tape we hold — not the historical book, which ran different exits.

(2) The router's operational grade is NOT in this section. That is §2.6's job and I have not repeated it. What is here is a different question: whether the instruments we grade the router with can be trusted. Three of them cannot.

(3) Gold is priced two ways and only one of them counts. Every gold study on this desk to date charged $1.50 per round trip and raced on the trade tape, which quietly assumes you were filled at the last traded price on both legs. MGC's median spread is 0.30pt = $3.00, and both our entries and our closes cross. The honest cost is $7.50 per round trip. Where it matters I show both, and the honest one decides.

(4) MGC is $10.00 a point, MNQ is $2.00. Every gold dollar below uses $10.

(5) Thin is thin. 34 tick-days for grind, 32 contiguous days for gold's quote tape, 185 out-of-sample gold sessions. Nothing here is a year of live trading and I say so at each table rather than once at the top.

1 · THE STANDING GRIND LEAD — which enable-mechanism actually works?

Your standing question is: what best captures grind's trend-day upside while killing its chop-churn — (a) trend-day-only, (b) its own entry trend-confirmation or veto, or (c) the current ER-0.35 floor? I judged this on live/managed grind only, never on the unmanaged grind_fast shadow, which has no stop discipline and reads nothing like the gate we run.

1.1 — Before choosing: option (c) does not exist

There is no ER-0.35 floor on grind. I imported the live module rather than trusting the documentation:

—ATR_FLOOR = {'grind_long': 22.0, 'capitulation_long': 10.0}an ATR floor of 22 is the ONLY entry filter grind carries

So the real choice is between (a), (b), and the thing that is actually deployed. I have scored (c) anyway, as the hypothetical it is, because it keeps getting proposed and it deserves a number rather than an opinion.

Two things to take from the control before any filter touches it. It is positive — the deployed ATR floor is already doing real work, and "grind loses money" is not true of the configuration we actually run. And it is fragile: three trades are the entire result. A 30% win rate with a 2.5-to-1 payoff is exactly the shape you told me not to kill on win rate alone, so I have judged everything below on expectancy and robustness. But a result that dies when you remove its best three fires is not something to enlarge — it is something to make sturdier, and that is what the rest of this chapter is for.

Two notes on that last column before you read it. For the day-level rules the null is dropping the same number of DAYS at random, and for the entry-level rules it is dropping the same number of FIRES at random — a day rule removes whole days, so scoring it against a per-trade null would flatter it. Both are 500-draw Monte Carlo estimates, so read them to the nearest few percent. And hold the two green (a) rows lightly until §1.4, which shows that most of what makes them look that good is the window I measured them over, not the market.

Option (b) is dead and the cause of death is the placebo. Every single entry-level confirmation and veto is beaten by 50% to 71% of random removals of the same number of trades — which is to say, they carry no information at all beyond "trade less". Four of the five also make the total worse, two of them turning a positive book negative. There is no version of "make grind confirm its own direction before it enters" that works on this evidence.

Option (c) is worse than doing nothing, even as a hypothetical. The 0.35 cell looks alright at $27.67 a fire until you notice it is 15 trades, it does not survive stripping its best three, and 28% of random draws of 15 fires beat it. That is now the fourth time this desk has tested "fix grind with an efficiency filter" and it has failed every time. It should stop being proposed.

1.4 — And then the finding that breaks the best-looking rule

Option (a) looks superb in that table: roundtrip ≥ 0.65 gives $70 a fire, survives everything, and only 1% of random draws beat it. It is also not deployable, and the reason is a measurement artefact I introduced myself. The window I measured "the day's character" over ended at the day's first fire — which means its length varies with the day, and the length of a quiet stretch before the first signal is itself a fact about the day. In production the router must decide before it knows when the first fire will be. So I recomputed exactly the same rule on a fixed clock cut instead:

The best runnable version — measure the day's roundtrip at the 13:30Z open, arm grind only above 0.55 — still beats the control, +$1,518 against +$922 on half the fires, and its worst leave-one-day-out fold is positive. But 22% of random 16-day selections beat it, and at 11:30Z the whole family is underwater. That is a rule with a real but modest effect wrapped in a lot of noise, and it is nowhere near the +$2,826 headline. Trend-day arming is the best of your three options and it is still not good enough to ship.

1.5 — The answer nobody asked for: grind's money is not on trend days at all

This is the part that changes the question. I split the 159 fires by the regime at the fire — ATR terciles against the 30-minute efficiency, exactly the segmentation your backtest rule demands, everything causal:

Read the top and the bottom rows together, because between them they invert the premise of the whole question. Grind's upside is not on clean trend days — clean trend is its worst regime, green on one day in seven. Its money comes from violent-whipsaw tape and from the building phase, and its bleed is ordinary mid-volatility chop. Eight fires is a thin cell and I am not going to pretend otherwise, but one green day in seven and −$82 a fire is a direction, not a rounding error.

That also explains, mechanically, why every option-(b) rule failed. An entry-level efficiency confirmation selects for exactly the CLEAN_TREND cell where grind loses the most. You were asking me to filter towards the thing that costs it money.
