The last two rows close a question that has been open since the last cycle, which reframed this whole lead as "the real question is whether 22 is the right floor". The answer is no — the floor is not the lever. Raising it to 26 or to 32 makes grind worse on every robustness column and is beaten by roughly half of all random draws. What matters is not how violent the tape is, it is the joint state of volatility and efficiency.

And the 13:00Z hour deserves its own sentence because it is the single cleanest fact in this chapter. Grind's fires in the US-open hour: 50 of them, across 25 separate days, −$1,618, green on 8 days of 25, an 18% win rate against 30% everywhere else. Strip its three worst fires and it is still −$1,022, so it is not one bad morning. Grind is a continuation gate and 13:30Z is the one moment of the day guaranteed to break continuation.

The honest limits on (d) and (e), because they are not small

Neither clears a 5% placebo. (d) is beaten by 10% of random 104-fire draws and (e) by 7%. That is much better than everything in §1.3 and it is not proof.

The second half is much weaker than the first. (d) makes +$2,072 in the first 17 days and +$238 in the last 17. The effect is real in both halves and it is nine times smaller in the recent one. That could be regime, it could be decay, and 17 days cannot tell you which.

(e) was chosen after I looked at the hour table. Its 7% placebo is not charged for that search, and "bench three specific hours" at 3% is charged even less. I am reporting (e) because it corroborates (d) — both say the damage is where continuation breaks — not as a rule to ship on its own.

(d) was not chosen on P&L. The five-way regime taxonomy is the one we already use for gold and it was written down before it was scored here. That is the main reason I trust it more than the clock rule, even though the clock rule scores better.

Verdict: SHADOW, not LIVE. Put (d) into the shadow book as a regime-gated grind arm — it is free, it is riskless, and it needs about four more weeks before the second-half number means anything. What would promote it: the second half reaching parity with the first, and a placebo under 5% on a sample that includes days I have not looked at. What would kill it: NORMAL_CHOP turning green, or CLEAN_TREND turning green, on the new days.

2 · THE WEEK'S INSTRUMENT LEADS — three scoreboards that are measuring the wrong thing

The router's operational grade lives in §2.6 and I have not repeated a line of it. This is the adjacent question, and it is the one the scope keeps asking: can the instruments we grade with be trusted? Three of this week's cannot, and each failure is a different shape.

2.1 — The exit selector grades a switched-off feature, and its model disagrees with the book by the SIGN

Friday 08-28 is the only day this week with a real selector scorecard, and it reads 13 trades, 4 optimal picks, $1,576 of regret, selector P&L −$600. Six of those thirteen rows are the tournament's six real trades. Here is the model's number beside what the account actually banked:

Trade (08-28)exit the selector says was chosenselector's P&Lselector's best modeits P&L"regret"WHAT THE DESK ACTUALLY BOOKED
capitulation_long_Awide−$59.0scalp+$113.5$172.5+$69.50
capitulation_long_Bwide−$59.0scalp+$113.5$172.5+$79.00
grind_long_Awide−$57.5mid+$117.5$175.0+$41.50
grind_long_Bwide−$57.5mid+$117.5$175.0+$22.00
abs_veto_long_Awide−$57.0mid+$139.5$196.5+$45.00
abs_veto_long_Bwide−$57.0mid+$134.0$191.0+$73.00
the six legs together—−$347.00——$1,082.50+$330.00

Six trades. The desk made money on all six. The selector's model says it lost money on all six. That is a $677 gap with the sign reversed on every row, and $1,082 of the day's $1,576 "regret" headline is computed inside it.

Three separate reasons, all of them structural rather than a bug:

Why the model and the book disagreeEvidence
The "chosen" mode is a reconstruction, not an observation. It calls SlotStrategy._regime_mode() to guess what a selector would have picked.the desk does not run any of the four modes — it runs the A/B scale-out slate
Every mode reprices on a hard-coded 1.0×ATR stop, so all four arms share one stop the desk does not use.stop_atr_mult=1.0 in all four branches of _mode_exit
Four of the six legs exited on MANUAL_CLAIM — your finger, not the gate's exit stack. No model exit can reproduce those.grind_long_A/B and abs_veto_long_B all closed MANUAL_CLAIM between 14:50 and 14:51Z

And underneath all of it: the feature being graded is switched off. I imported scaleout_slots() and all twelve sub-slots return adaptive_exit=False. So the scorecard is a simulation of a disabled feature, priced with a stop the desk does not use, on trades a human closed by hand. The $1,576 is not a measurement of anything.

2.2 — The router's net-value number is one-sided by construction

This one is easy to miss because the number it produces is usually reasonable. router_value = saved − missed, and both terms are computed entirely from SUPPRESSED-OPEN lines — that is, from signals the router BLOCKED. The only thing it records about an ARMED gate is leakage, and leakage counts losers only. There is no term anywhere in the file for a winner that an arm produced.

Friday 2026-08-28what the nightly recordedwhat actually happened
blocked signals repriced34—
blocked losses saved+$1,888—
blocked wins missed−$2,005—
net router value, as printed−$117—
P&L from the three gates the router ARMED at 14:45Z and 16:00Znot counted — no term exists+$330.00, six for six
honest net for the day—+$213

A $447 swing and a sign flip on the one day this week the desk actually traded. The fix is small — add realised P&L from managed gates while ON to the value term — and until it is made, every daily router value on record is a lower bound on days the router armed anything, and exactly right on days it armed nothing. Most days it armed nothing, which is why nobody has noticed.

2.3 — The blanket stand-down out-scored the selective router, four to one per day

The week splits itself into a natural experiment nobody designed. Monday and Tuesday the whole six-gate roster was stood down. The stand-down was lifted on Wednesday 08-26 and the router held full authority for the last three days. Same instrument, same scalp-2R ruler, same nightly:

On this week's tape, doing nothing at all beat doing something clever by roughly four to one per day. I want to be careful with that, because it is two days against three, on different tapes, on a ruler that is known to be more generous than the live desk, and §2.2 above says the authority days are understated by the +$330 the arms actually earned (which lifts them to +$186/day, still short). It is not a recommendation to stand the desk down. It is a challenge to the bar: whatever the router is worth, it has to clear "switch everything off", and this week it did not.

2.5 — It armed a gate this morning on a tape with nothing on it

Not a mid-week lead — it happened while I was writing this, and it is the sharpest example of the failure mode in the file. At 2026-08-29 07:20:25Z, a Saturday, roughly ten hours into a CME halt that runs until Sunday 22:00Z, the router armed capitulation_long. Its own words:

2026-08-29T07:20:25Z — verbatim from the trial log

"07:20Z LONDON, the desk's only positive block — flat, healthy=true, halted=false, day total +0.0, 0 bars in 45min so NO segment read (direction rule silent), DAY BIAS insufficient-bars, meter 50 is an explicit NO READ … so I route on the tape and the tape is empty; correcting my own last four ticks, which asserted capitulation_long 'stays on' when the switch has in fact read off … it does not need a fresh positive case to sit armed and I am arming it rather than under-arming London…"

Three things are wrong at once and they compound. It reads halted=false through a halt. It calls a dead Saturday "LONDON, the desk's only positive block", and that phrase — a true statement about the desk's session P&L — is what supplies the arming pressure. And the actual justification is a correction of its own state misread, which is a fact about the router, not a fact about the market.

The dollars are $0 because there is no market, and the router will get 460 more ticks to change its mind before the reopen. The lead is not the loss, it is the mechanism: the Asia block expires on a clock boundary at 07:00Z, and the moment it does, the "London is our best block" reasoning switches on with nothing to read. One arm in three weekend-days is a rate, not an incident — but it is a rate that only needs to be wrong once, on a Sunday-night reopen gap, to matter. Recommendation for the Saturday card: give the router a calendar. A weekend and holiday check is about fifteen lines and it removes an entire class of decision made on zero information.

3 · ★★ GOLD — the required chapter, written for someone who has seen none of it

We have been capturing COMEX gold — MGC, both the quote tape and the order book — since 2026-08-04, and you asked for gates that work on it. Nothing gold-related has ever gone live and nothing here proposes to. This chapter exists because two findings from the 08-14 session changed the shape of the gold problem, and because both of them needed testing much harder than the session that produced them could manage. One of them survived that test and got stronger. The other one died, and it died on evidence that was already sitting on the disk.

3.1 — Why gold gets a fresh chapter when six attacks are already refuted

The honest starting point is that gold has beaten us six times. On 2026-08-05 a full session closed six separate attacks, and none of them failed on thin data — they failed on mechanism:

AttackHow it died
a momentum / direction gate5 of 72 cells positive; the best strips to $16; always SHORT (−$532) BEAT the directed gate (−$1,274)
arm, then confirm after a delaythe confirmed side is a coin flip — 48–50% across all 24 cells
filter it with the live router metersplacebo-controlled and beaten by 31–80% of random removals
use the L2 book for direction, or as a vetowell powered, and the edge flips sign across five disjoint samples
fade extension on a clockHurst exponent on our own gold tape is 0.489 — a random walk
thrust-continuationcatches 22 of 22 runs and the losers are statistically indistinguishable from the winners

The only thing that ever survived a robustness test was an oracle day-filter — given foresight of which days contain a run, +$779. That is your "let the router switch it off" idea, and it is an upper bound, not a result. So why is this different from a seventh sweep? Because the two 08-14 findings are not new thresholds on old mechanisms. One is a statement about the SHAPE of gold's moves that changes which exit you should even be testing. The other is a different trade entirely — one position a day, held to a clock, which is not a gate at all. Neither had been tried before, so neither is a retry.

3.2 — Before any gold number: three things were wrong with the ruler

I could not re-derive anything until I fixed the measuring stick, and two of the three faults are new this month. They matter enough that they would be a finding on their own.

Fault one — on 2026-08-19 a backfill quietly put four extra timeframes into the lake, and nothing filters them. The lake's bars view is a plain union over every parquet file in data/tape/bars/<symbol>/. Someone dropped backfill_1day, backfill_1hour, backfill_1min and backfill_5mins in there. Any study that reads bars without timeframe='5s' now silently resamples daily and hourly bars as if they were five-second ones.

timeframe in data/tape/bars/MGC/rowsdistinct daysspan
5s — our own capture, the only one anything should read292,232182026-08-05 → 2026-08-28
1min — arrived 08-19357,6923202025-07-27 → 2026-08-18
5mins — arrived 08-1926,4191382025-09-29 → 2026-08-19
1hour — arrived 08-1910,2335472024-10-30 → 2026-08-19
1day — arrived 08-196916912023-11-30 → 2026-08-19

The damage is a look-ahead, not just noise. Resampling that union to one minute takes high = max(...) across all of them, so the 10:00 minute inherits the high of the 5-minute bar stamped 10:00 — a number not known until 10:05. Measured on the July archive days: 4,826 of 10,881 minutes (44.4%) carry an inflated range, mean inflation 2.089pt on a bar whose clean range averages 2.099pt. The leak is worth roughly a whole bar. And the audit's own control — the August days, which used to be 5-second-only and were designed to read zero — now reads 9,469 inflated minutes. That is the backfill landing, visible in a test built before it existed. MNQ has the identical four files, so this is not a gold problem; it is a lake problem, and it is on the Saturday card.

Fault two — gold has been priced at a fifth of its real cost. Every MGC study charged $1.50 per round trip and raced exits on the trade tape. Our entries are marketable limits that cross and our closes are market orders that cross, so both legs pay the spread:

The spread is between a quarter and a half of one R on this instrument. On MNQ, where 1R is $30–$60 and the spread is a quarter of a point, you can get away with ignoring it. On gold you cannot, and every prior gold verdict is affected.

Fault three — a third of the new days are dead. The backfill's 320 MGC minute-days are not all real tape. I measured the share of minutes with zero price change on each day; a live gold minute changes price about 96% of the time.

Once the dead days are dropped the extension is genuine, and that is what lets §3.4 do what it does.

3.3 — LEAD ONE: gold's runs are grinds, not thrusts, and the EXIT was the cap — SURVIVES

The 08-14 claim, in your terms: gold's big moves are long slow grinds rather than sharp thrusts, so a trailing exit gets shaken out of them; boarding was never the problem, the exit was; and the ceiling moves from about $83 a week on a 2.5×ATR trail to about $346 a week on a wide stop held for hours. If true it inverts the order of the whole gold problem, because it means the filter question — the one that has failed six times — only becomes worth solving after the exit is fixed.

I re-derived it on 32 contiguous trading days of the 250ms quote book (2026-07-16 → 2026-08-28, 5.6M snapshots, no gaps), with minute bars built from the quote mid so there is no construction seam, and every exit raced spread-honestly — a long's stop triggers when the bid breaks it and the long exits at the bid, never at the midpoint.

The description of the tape holds. Defining a run as a directional leg worth at least $300 gross on one lot, ended by a 34% retrace:

Top five: median efficiency 0.20, median duration 2.9 hours, 3 of 5 last two hours or more. Across all 55 runs found: median efficiency 0.30, median duration 118 minutes, 49% last two hours or more. An efficiency of 0.20 means price travels five times the net distance it ends up covering — a grind, exactly as claimed (the 08-14 read was 0.23 on a shorter window). A trailing stop set to a couple of ATRs cannot survive that.

Now the test that matters. I built one boarding rule and then changed nothing about it: 165 signals, entered a minute after the bar that produced them, one per hour at most. Only the exit changes between rows, so any difference is the exit and nothing else.

Notice also that a wide trail does not rescue it (−$699): it is not the width, it is the trailing. Gold wants board-once, hold-wide, leave-on-a-clock.

The mirror is negative at every single cell and gets more negative as the real thing gets better — which is what a genuinely directional entry looks like and is the opposite of what drift-harvesting looks like. Random-minute entries are negative too. This is the strongest gold result on the desk and the first one to pass its own adversarial control.

Four things wrong with it, all of them mine to say

The median trade LOSES, and loses more as the total improves — −$60 at 3h, −$75 at 12h. The win rate FALLS from 38% to 24% as the number gets better. Everything is in the tail. You would sit through long strings of small losses waiting for the one that pays, and on a 2-lot 20–30 trade month that is a genuinely uncomfortable equity curve.

A 12-hour hold breaks your standing rule. "NEVER HOLD OVERNIGHT. EVER." A gold trade opened at 14:00Z and held twelve hours is open at 02:00Z. The best cell that fits inside a session is 5×ATR, 3h: +$370, or $58/week — real, and a sixth of the headline. The gap between $58 and $422 a week is entirely the overnight rule, and that is a decision for you, not a finding for me.

The boarding rule was chosen, not swept. Efficiency ≥ 0.50 with a 20-minute net of at least 1.5×ATR and an hour of dead time between signals. It is a reasonable rule and it is one rule. The exit matrix is honest because the entries are held fixed across it; the entry itself has not been robustness-tested and I am not claiming it has.

Thirty-two days, one instrument, one direction of gold. The tape fell overall across the window. 165 trades is a decent n and 6.4 weeks is not a long time.

3.4 — LEAD TWO: the MGC day rider and its beautiful plateau — REFUTED

This was the most promising shape gold had ever shown, and it is worth saying exactly why it looked so good, because the failure is instructive rather than embarrassing.

The idea: one trade a day, no gate at all. At 14:30Z run the live drift detector on the first hour of the US session; if it reports a confirmed direction, take two lots that way and hold to the 20:40Z flat, which is when you are watching anyway. The thresholds were derived properly — not swept for P&L, but by finding what percentile MNQ's live constants occupy in MNQ's own distribution and reading gold's value at the same percentile, because the transferable quantity is the selectivity, not the number.

And the sensitivity grid was a plateau, which is the thing you are supposed to want. Not a peak with cliffs either side — every neighbouring cell positive too. Here it is, re-derived today on our own capture with the honest $7.50 cost:

Every cell positive. Every cell survives stripping its best day. Direction holds to the flat four times in five. The spread cost barely dents it because there is only one round trip a day. Fifteen for fifteen becomes zero for fifteen. The direction-hold rate, which was the whole reason to believe in it, falls from 78–85% to 49–54%. That is a coin flip, and I tested it as one: at the best out-of-sample cell the direction held 34 times in 63, and the probability of doing that well or better on a fair coin is 0.307. Meanwhile always short — no detector, no thresholds, no thought — made +$11,090 across the same 185 days. The filtered version loses money where the dumb constant makes it, which is precisely how the momentum gate died back in August.

One green segment out of eight, and it is quiet opens rather than active ones — the opposite of the story. It survives stripping its best day (+$2,720), which is more than most things here manage, and it is one of three ATR cells I chose after looking at all three. That is a PARK, not a find.

The lesson, and it applies to everything else in this report

The plateau logic was applied correctly in August. All 15 cells positive, the peak cell not shipped, the derivation done distributionally rather than by fitting P&L — that was good work and it would catch a threshold fluke every time. It cannot catch a sample fluke, because every cell of the grid is scored on the same sixteen days. A plateau tests sensitivity to the THRESHOLD. It says nothing at all about sensitivity to the SAMPLE, and on this desk the sample is almost always the binding constraint. When you next see fifteen green cells, the question to ask is not "is it a peak or a plateau" — it is "how many independent days is that grid standing on".

3.5 — The coil bouncer — REFUTED, and the mixed-timeframe leak is what killed it

The coil bouncer was the strongest standalone gold gate: when the last 20 minutes' range shrinks to 0.60× its own two-hour median, fade whichever edge price is sitting on back to the middle of the coil. It had a genuinely good report card on 08-14 — n=154, +$470.42, a positive median trade of +$7.75, placebo beaten 0 times out of 12, and a mirror control at −$923.75. It is also mechanically distinct from the refuted fader: that one faded EXTENSION, this one trades COMPRESSION.

I re-ran the desk's own script, changing exactly one thing — the bar loader now filters timeframe='5s'. Same rule, same exit, same placebo, same cost model, ten days more tape:

Coil bounceras reported 2026-08-14re-run with the clean loaderwhat happened
days of tape1828—
trades154291—
net at $1.50/RT+$470.42−$413.69sign flips

placebo — 12 random-time setsbeaten 0/12beaten 6/12a coin flip — no information

green days—9 / 27—
and at the TRUE $7.50 cost, 291 trades pay a further…—−$1,746—

Cause of death: the placebo test, 6 of 12. And the mechanism of the error is specific and worth remembering. The coil rule is a RANGE rule — it compares a 20-minute high-minus-low against a 2-hour median of the same thing. That is the single most look-ahead-sensitive quantity there is, and the mixed-timeframe union inflated 44.4% of July's minute ranges by roughly a whole bar. A range rule fed inflated ranges finds coils that were not coils and edges that were not edges. The gate was measuring the bug.

3.6 — The London-open break fade — REFUTED, on the cost model alone

Gold's session-open breaks fail: continuation after the 06:00Z opening range wins 6.2% of the time. So fade them. On 08-14 that gave n=16 and +$502.42, beaten by 0 of 7 shifted anchors, though the median trade already lost. Re-run through the desk's own script with the clean loader:

This is the cleanest kill in the file and it needs one sentence. The gate earns $4.93 a trade. The spread it never paid is $6.00 a trade. Its entire edge is smaller than the cost it was not being charged, and the honest net over 26 days is −$27.86. It does still beat the other two anchors, so the shape is not nothing — but a shape whose expectancy is below its own transaction cost is not a trade, it is a subsidy.

3.8 — The cost of finding out

The 08-14 session closed with a line I want to correct rather than repeat: "the missing ingredient is DAYS, not configurations." That was right, and it turned out to be cheaper to test than anyone expected — the days had already arrived, in a backfill five days later that nobody announced and nothing used. Here is what that cost and what it bought:

What we thought we neededWhat was actually availableWhat it cost to use it
More gold sessions. 16–18 was too thin to promote anything.253 usable MGC minute-days already in the lake since 2026-08-19, verified against our own capture to 0.0pt on every shared July closeone staleness filter and one instrument check — about an hour
A contiguous gold tape without the 07-18 → 08-04 hole.32 contiguous days of 250ms quotes, because the depth capture kept running through the window the L1 mirror did notalready built — it is what §3.3 runs on
More configurations to sweep.Nothing. The day rider's grid was already a plateau. More cells would have made it look better and told us less.—

So the corrected version of the lesson: the missing ingredient was days, and the reason we did not have them was not that they did not exist — it was that nothing checked whether they did. The backfill sat in the lake for ten days, silently corrupting every study that read it and silently holding the answer to the one question those studies could not settle. That is the pattern this desk keeps hitting: an instrument that is quietly wrong is worse than one that is loudly broken, because a wrong number looks exactly like a finding.

What gold needs next is not more sweeps and not more days. It needs the run-boarding entry — the only thing that has passed a mirror — put into the shadow book with a session-bounded exit, and it needs someone to spend the 12 untouched L2-only days on it as a genuine out-of-sample leg. That is a Saturday afternoon, not a project.

P2.6 ROUTER OPERATION REVIEW — the desk's #1 lever, graded on the week's money

Garrath — the headline is uncomfortable and it is the most useful thing in this section. The router's own book made money this week and the desk still lost −$1,246.94. Every trade the router had authority over — all six of them, all on Thursday — won: +$330.00, 6 for 6. The −$1,576.94 that swamped it came from day_rider, 26 trades in a book the router cannot see and cannot switch off. So "was the router good this week" and "did the desk make money this week" are two different questions with two different answers, and conflating them is the single easiest way to draw the wrong conclusion from this week. The second thing: for five of the week's eight days the router was managing a book the operator had already stood down — your 08-20 stand-down text sat in its prompt through 1,802 consecutive ticks until the router itself flagged it as stale at 08-27 13:05Z. Third, and this is the number I'd act on: the router's direction reads were right and its latency was the dominant error. Thursday's arm was 20m17s late and the lateness cost $205–$705 against +$181.50 banked. Fourth: the untradeable-day meter is dead. Scored the way it actually runs — intraday, before the day is over — it has no discrimination at any decision hour on any cutoff (ρ = +0.17 / −0.09 / +0.11), and the tempting "move the cutoff to 45" fix fails strip-the-best-2 with a sign flip. Fifth: the threshold sweep says leave the thresholds alone. ER 0.15 / NET 30 sits in the middle of a genuine 3-cell plateau on both universes. The money in that sweep is in the timing knobs, and the timing story is corroborated independently by the lateness finding.

What survived, in order of how much I'd trust it
  1. The router's own book is 6-for-6 at +$330.00 this week, and its held benches priced out at +$1,224.38 saved against $241.07 of measurable error. On the calls that can be graded, it is winning.
  2. The shipped thresholds are already at the robust optimum. ER 0.15 / NET 30 is the centre of a 3-cell plateau (+461 / +492 / +428 live-managed; +1,076 / +1,083 / +1,070 full-historical). Raising ER above 0.15 is strictly worse on both sets. Do not touch them.
  3. Latency is the biggest single error term on the desk's #1 lever — measured at $205–$705 on one afternoon, larger than anything on the scoreboard. Independently, the sweep's joint-best wants step 15m → 5m. Two unrelated methods pointing the same way is the strongest signal in this section.
  4. Benching abs_veto_short is the router's proven edge — +$1,208.50 saved across every nightly on record, more than every other gate's bench combined. Benching capitulation_long and grind_long is value-destroying (−$242.80 and −$156.20).
  5. The untradeable meter is REFUTED as built — and that is a survivor, because it stops us tuning a cutoff on a number that is reading the day it is supposed to be forecasting.
Read this before any number below

Every dollar figure is pnl_usd from gazbot7.db, which is net of the $1.50-per-round-trip fee already — nothing here double-charges costs. One row is excluded desk-wide (BADFILL:stale_price_30pt_outside_book_20260821). Bench savings are counterfactual: the benched gate never traded, so its "saving" is a tick-replay of what it wanted to do, and it is a different ruler from a booked fill. I never sum the two into one headline. And the week is thin — 6 managed trades and 18 switch changes is not a sample you can conclude much from. Where a number rests on n < 10 I say so on the row.

The one thing in this table that is not what it looks like

The +$50.48 bench of abs_veto_long on 08-28 is credited to the wrong thing. The bench saved money, yes — but the tape hit both of the gate's own targets, and the loss only exists because the desk's stop is too tight: MAE was 1.149×ATR against a 1.0×ATR stop, and at k = 1.25 that same trade is +$100. That is a saving earned by a stop-width bug, not by the router's read. The router read the direction wrong and got paid for it. If we widen the stop — which the exit lab wants — this "saving" flips to a cost, and the same will be true of several other cells in this table. It belongs on the scoreboard as a $ fact and nowhere near a claim about the router's judgement.

Is it net-positive? Yes, but only just, and the margin is 6%. The router saved $47,907 and missed $45,060 across 20 days. It is winning 51.5% of the money it touches. That is a coin-flip with a small tilt, and it means the ordering of individual days is mostly noise — do not read a −$543 Wednesday as a bad Wednesday.

Is it over-benching? On the aggregate, no — per gate, yes, on two of them. "Over-benching" shows up as missed > saved, and that happened on 9 of the 18 scoring days. But the per-gate table in section 2 localises it precisely: capitulation_long (−$242.80) and grind_long (−$156.20) are where the over-benching lives, and grind_long is 46% of every blocked trade on the desk.

Where it is leaking — and why the zeros lie

leakage_n = 0 for every day this week. That is not a clean bill of health. The leakage universe is only the gates the router manages, and the two it actually watches most closely (capitulation_long, rgv_short) barely trade — 22 blocked trades each across the whole file. A zero here means an empty universe, not an absence of leaks. The all-time leak of −$1,469 over 28 trades is what the measurement can see, and it is concentrated on 07-27→07-29 and 08-12.

And the real leak this week is not in this table at all. It is day_rider: 26 trades, −$1,576.94, in a book with no router switch, no gate, and no entry in any nightly. The router's managed universe covered 6 of the desk's 32 trades this week — 19% of the flow and 21% of the gross P&L. That is the biggest single fact about router value in this report.

The joint best over 900 configs — and why I am not recommending it

Both universes independently pick the identical config — that is a real signal, and the thresholds are not where its money comes from. ER stays at 0.15 and NET moves 30→20, which we already know is inside the plateau and worth ~$0. All of the +$440–$502 is in the three timing knobs: window 30→45m, step 15→5m, hold 2→3.

MODERATE anti-overfit recommendation

Ship nothing on the thresholds. ER 0.15 / NET 30 stays. They are on a plateau, the "improvement" from NET 20 is $31 on 40 days, and moving a live threshold to capture $31 is exactly how a desk overfits.

The timing change is a genuine candidate but it is NOT deployable on this evidence alone. "4 days helped / 0 hurt" out of 40 means n = 4 — 36 of the 40 days are unaffected because the router never acted on them. A 4-day sample cannot carry a live config change, and I will not pretend otherwise.

What makes it worth doing anyway is that a completely independent measurement says the same thing. The 08-28 lateness finding (section 7) prices the actuation delay at $205–$705 on one afternoon — measured on the live tape, not in a sweep, and larger than the whole 40-day timing gain. Two unrelated methods both saying "the router is too slow" is the strongest conclusion in this section. The step is also the safest knob: it changes how often the router looks, not what it decides.

⚠ Saturday-deploy caveat. The 40 days are one summer RANGE regime, the trades are thin, and they are partly already hand- and router-gated — so the router is being scored on a tape it helped create. Everything here is an illustrative lower bound. Any change is a Saturday/operator call, and it should be re-run after a TREND week before anything touches the thresholds. If you deploy one thing, deploy the step; leave ER, NET, window and hold exactly where they are.

Does the 65 cutoff want tuning? The tempting answer, and why it is a trap

On 32 days of full-day scores the blend does look real (ρ = −0.294 vs the desk, −0.426 vs the tournament book), and the cutoff sweep is seductive:

cutoffdays sat outP&L avoideddays tradedP&L kept$ per traded day
3521−$5,95911+$1,830+$166

5013−$2,05419−$2,075−$109

That table says "move the cutoff from 65 to 45 and turn −$2,309 into +$2,123, a swing of +$4,432". It even passes a placebo test — shuffle the score labels across days 5,000 times and a random 45-cutoff beats +$2,123 only 2.8% of the time. Do not ship it. It dies twice:

robustness testresultverdict
Placebo (5,000 label shuffles)2.8%PASS
Leave-one-day-out (13 traded days)worst case +$950PASS — every single drop stays positive
Strip-the-best-2+$2,123 → −$160FAIL — SIGN FLIP. 07-30 (+$1,172) and 08-28 (+$1,110) are the whole edge
Scored the way it actually runs (intraday)no discrimination at any hourFAIL — and this one is fatal

Here is the fatal test, and it is the whole finding. Every number above scores the meter on the completed Paris day. But a stay-out call has to be made during the day. So I recomputed the meter using only the bars available at a real decision moment, and scored it against the P&L still to come after that moment:

decision momentdaysρ vs rest-of-day P&Lbest cutoff foundP&L kept at that cutoff
14:00Z (just after the US open)29+0.172none — every cutoff 35–75negative at all 8 cutoffs
16:00Z (mid-session)24−0.088nonenegative at all 8 cutoffs
18:00Z (late session)21+0.105nonenegative at all 8 cutoffs
Cause of death, stated plainly

The untradeable meter is a description of a day that has already happened, not a forecast of one that hasn't. Its full-day ρ of −0.294 is hindsight: ROUNDTRIP is |close − open| / range, which cannot be known until the close. Freeze it at any live decision hour and the correlation collapses to zero or flips positive (+0.172 / −0.088 / +0.105), and there is no cutoff, at any of the three hours, that leaves a profitable traded set.

Killed by: (a) the intraday test — no discrimination at any decision hour on any cutoff; (b) strip-the-best-2 — the full-day version's entire edge is two days and removing them flips the sign. It survives placebo and leave-one-day-out, which is exactly why it looked shippable and why those two tests were not enough.

So: the 65 cutoff does not want tuning. Tuning a cutoff on a number that reads the day it is supposed to predict just moves the hindsight around. The meter needs rebuilding on inputs knowable by 14:00Z, or retiring. Meanwhile it should not gate anything — and note that on 08-19 and 08-14 it would have sat us out of +$1,119.50 of real money.

A correction to the bad-call ledger's own account of this

The 08-29 ledger pass calls the session-limit outage "DAY 2" and says it "more than doubled" from yesterday's 7 ticks / 35 min. The log says otherwise. The first outage was 08-26, three days earlier, and that day had two — including a 13-tick / 65-minute hole in the middle of live RTH, nearly twice the size of the 08-28 one the ledger treats as the baseline. It is day 4, not day 2, and the worst live-session hole was on the day the ledger doesn't count. The trend is real and the ledger under-states it.

Every one of these is invisible to the usual instruments: systemd logs them as Deactivated successfully, and router_trial_log.txt carries no line at all — a bare gap that is indistinguishable from the designed 21:00–21:40Z skip. router_headless.log is the only witness. And because the fail-safe is benching-only, an outage is one-directional: the router cannot bench during the hole, so whatever is armed stays armed. On a shut tape that costs nothing. In a live 80-minute US-open hole it is the whole book.

The actuation-lag bill

This is the number I would put in front of everything else in this section.

event, 08-28$ basis
Banked by the 14:45:03Z arm+$181.50real fills, 6 trades, all winners
— worth on the gates' own exits+$266.10a MANUAL_CLAIM truncated the exit stack — the leg measures the operator's timing, not the gate's edge
Long side — 20m17s late−$166.55 to −$601.30floor = one slot holds one position, so the arm buys ONE trade; ceiling = all four pre-arm target-reaching legs
Short side — ~11 min late−$38.50 to −$103.36two benched abs_veto_short impulses that both hit target
TOTAL LATENESS COST, one afternoon−$205 to −$705against +$181.50 banked — the lag cost more than the call made

Quote the range, never the $601.30 alone. Those four long impulses are one trend sampled four times, not four independent opportunities, and one slot can only hold one position. The honest statement is: the router's direction reads were right on both sides, and its latency turned a right call into roughly break-even. Latency is now the dominant error term on the desk's #1 lever — it is a bigger number than anything on the GOOD/BAD scoreboard.

Architecture — two structural notes

The router is not the only writer of gate_switches.env, and it does not know it. open_hour_watch.py wrote an arm of abs_veto_short at 08-28 16:24:01Z; reactivate_gates arms three gates at 22:00:00Z nightly. The router's ABORT fail-safe (“no change”) is only safe while the router is the sole writer — during the 235 minutes it was blind this week, it was not.

And the stand-down text never expired. Your 08-20 instruction — only the day rider trades — was spliced into every router prompt as a comment and stayed there through 1,802 consecutive ticks over seven days, five of them after the tape had reopened. Nothing pruned it. The router itself broke the loop at 08-27 13:05Z: “the 08-20 stand-down text in my prompt is STALE.” That is a good outcome from a bad mechanism — it worked because the model noticed, not because anything checked. A carve-out comment with no expiry is a standing instruction, and this one cost the router five days of authority.

8 · Verdict and Saturday recommendations

Verdict

KEEP THE ROUTER. It is net-positive, it is not thrashing, and on the calls that can be graded it is winning. It turns a losing fader book into a winning one on both tested universes (−$302→+$190 live-managed; −$431→+$652 full-historical), its nightlies roll up to +$2,846 over 20 days, its book went 6-for-6 at +$330.00 this week, and its bad-call scoreboard improved to 64% GOOD on the week against 56% lifetime.

But three things are true at the same time and all three matter more than the scoreboard. (1) Its edge is one gate. 85% of all measured bench value is abs_veto_short; the other seven gates are worth 27 cents a blocked trade and two are negative. (2) Its errors are now timing, not direction. $205–$705 lost to a 20-minute delay on one afternoon, versus $241.07 of graded direction error all week. (3) Its scope is 19% of the desk. It managed 6 of 32 trades while the book it cannot see lost −$1,576.94.

What this section is NOT evidence for — read before acting

The router's own book took six trades this week. Six. All on one day, all long, all winners. That is not a sample, it is an anecdote, and nothing in section 1 or 2 should be read as a forward estimate of anything.

The 40-day sweep is one summer RANGE regime and the trades in it are partly already hand- and router-gated — the router is being scored on a tape it helped create. Every Δ in section 4 is an illustrative lower bound. The joint-best config rests on 4 days helped / 0 hurt out of 40.

Every bench "saving" is a counterfactual replayed on the tape, and several of them are sensitive to the stop width — the 08-28 +$50.48 flips to +$100 for the gate at k = 1.25. If the exit lab widens the stop, some of the savings in section 2 become costs. They are $ facts about what happened; they are not claims about the router's judgement.

And the one conclusion I would stake real money on is the smallest one: the router is too slow. It is the only finding here supported by two independent methods — a 900-config sweep and a live tape replay — that were not fitted to each other.

M1 The biggest runs on MNQ this week — did we show up?

Forget what the desk did this week — start from the raw tape. MNQ printed 65 runs of 1.5×ATR or bigger between 2026-08-23 22:00 and 2026-08-28 20:59 UTC (a 15-minute move of at least 55 points, against a typical 15-min range of 37). That is the whole tape, not a top-ten. We caught 2, we were positioned against 1, and we sat out 62. The runs we aligned with banked +$1,052.50 of honest money on the eight lots we actually took — against a $1,520 ceiling at that size, a 69.2% conversion — and the 62 we sat out left $10,278 on the table ($9,830 over 61 once the halt-straddling 08-26 20:46 window is removed; see HONEST MONEY below). The bleed is not the runs; it is the fading we do around them.

It read “+$1,052 — but that is only 277% of their $380 hindsight ceiling”. Two things wrong with one sentence. “Only 277%” reads as a shortfall when it is more than double; and the reason real money could exceed a hindsight ceiling at all is that the ceiling is ONE LOT and the book is not. The $ 1lot column above is deliberately one lot — it is a size-free measure of the move — while the desk took four lots into each caught run, across two different books. A percentage between those two is not a conversion rate; it is a lot-count.

And the Gate column under-named both. The 08-28 14:41 row credited grind_long_A with +$182: that is really all FOUR lots of the router arm — grind_long_A +$41.50, grind_long_B +$22.00, abs_veto_long_A +$45.00, abs_veto_long_B +$73.00 = +$181.50. The 08-27 13:39 row's +$871 is the day rider — a different book, which reads none of the router's switches — on four one-lot legs opened 13:42:06Z. And the 08-28 14:00 FOUGHT row's +$148 is both capitulation lots (+$69.50 and +$79.00).

Every row is a sat-out row because there is no gate on this instrument to catch or fight anything. The ceiling is what one lot would have made on a perfect entry and a perfect exit, so treat it as the size of the seat, never as money forgone. The next two movements ask what could fill it.

M2 THE IDLE-GATE LAB — could the gates we already own have caught the runs we sat out?

Movement 1 has just shown you 62 runs this week that the desk sat out entirely, worth $10,278 if every one had been caught perfectly. The obvious question — and the cheapest one, because it needs no new code — is whether the six gates we already own would have caught any of them had they simply been left armed. This lab answers it by replaying every one of those runs second by second: 36,600 decision-seconds of real quotes, each gate's own deciders, each gate's own A/B exit pair, and the desk's real cost of $1.50 a round trip.

THE ANSWER, IN FOUR NUMBERS

1. Fired exactly as they are configured today, the gates take 32 lots into the runs and lose $−741.50 ($−23.17/lot, 18.8% win). 2. Strip every constraint the live mechanism imposes — the "ungated" layer, which is the gates' raw pattern with nothing filtering it — and they take 114 lots for $−168.50. Almost break-even, on 3.6× the volume. 3. Now keep only the fires that pointed the same way as the run: 26 lots, $+1,218.50, 65.4% win, $+46.87/lot. 4. And that is the trap, because the direction is only knowable afterwards. The gates do not know which way the run will go — that is what “sat out” means. Reading number 3 as an opportunity is reading the answer off the back of the exam paper.

§1  The population — what we are replaying

Every sat-out run from this week's census freeze: 62 runs, $10,278 of hindsight ceiling, 36,600 decision-seconds. ★ REV2 — which figure this lab replayed, stated, and what it costs. All 62, including the 08-26 20:46 window, whose 180 five-second bars straddle the 21:00–22:00Z CME halt and are therefore 75 minutes of clock across a closed market rather than a 15-minute move (Movement 1's census now marks it; Part 1's run chart shows the gap). Drop it and the population is 61 runs and $9,830. Here is what that actually changes, measured rather than asserted: — MECH: nothing at all. 32 lots, −$741.50, identical. The section's headline number does not depend on the bad window. — UNGATED: it gets WORSE without it. 114 lots −$168.50 becomes 112 lots −$264.00, because the two fires inside that window were both winners. — And it does move one verdict in §4. Those two fires are grind_long_A and _B, entered 20:44:20Z and closed 20:48 and 20:49 — on live tape, before the halt, at +$38.00 and +$57.50. They are real trades; it is the run's label that is the artefact. Remove them and grind_long's in-direction book goes from 10 lots at +$20.10 to 8 lots at +$13.19, which drops it below its own random-entry control (+$17.88) and takes §4's like-for-like count from 3 of 5 to 2 of 5. This is the SAME freeze Movement 1 reports — 65 runs, 2 caught, 1 fought, 62 sat out — so a per-run number here lines up with a per-run number there. (Last cycle's Movement 2 was computed on a superseded freeze and had to carry a banner saying its run list did not match the rest of the report. That is fixed: this section was recomputed on the 08-28 freeze.)

§2  The scoreboard — two layers, and why both are printed

§3  The in-direction number is an oracle — here is what it is worth and why you cannot have it

The single most seductive line in this lab is the ungated in-direction book: 26 lots, $+1,218.50, 65.4% win, $+46.87/lot. It looks like a strategy. It is not: in-direction means “the fire agreed with where the run subsequently went”, which is information from the future. The honest version of that book is the ALL-fires line right above it — 114 lots for $−168.50 — because at the moment of the fire, both books are the same book.

It is printed anyway, and stress-tested below, for one reason: if even the oracle version were negative, the gates would be dead and no selector could rescue them. It is positive, so the question “could something have picked the right ones in advance?” stays open — and Movement 3 is where that question gets asked properly. What follows is how much of that oracle survives contact with robustness.

§4  The random-entry control — the test that decides whether any of this is a gate at all

The kill test. If you had shown up at a random second inside the same 10-minute pre-ignition window, in the run's own direction, with the same gate's exits and the same costs — what would that have paid? Anything a gate earns has to beat this, because the gate's claim is that its trigger matters, not that being long a run pays. Pool: every 10th decision-second of every sat-out run, per gate.

And note the AGAINST column, which is the same control pointed the wrong way. Where a gate's number sits between the two, what it is measuring is the run, not the gate.

MOVEMENT 2 — VERDICT

No. The gates we own would not have caught this week's runs, and arming them into the runs costs $−741.50 on 32 lots. That is the third cycle in a row this lab has returned the same answer against a different week of tape, which is the most useful thing about it: the finding does not depend on which runs are in the census.

Three things follow, and only the third is new this week:

  1. The bench is earning its keep. Every gate benched into this week's run windows saved money by being benched. Nothing on the action card should propose re-arming one on the strength of a missed run.
  2. No threshold rescues them. A 724-cell sweep that relaxes one constraint at a time finds no cell that is both positive and more than three trades wide.
  3. ★ And the random-entry control returns a NULL — it cannot separate the triggers from chance in either direction. REV2 — restated Rev1 of this section said “not one gate's trigger beats it, 0 of 6”. That compared a control which had been handed the run's direction against the gate's both-directions number, and it loses by construction. Scored consistently (§4): in-direction the gates beat the control on 3 of 5, direction-blind on 4 of 5, and rgv_short never fired so it cannot be scored at all. But the in-direction lot counts are 2, 2, 6, 6 and 10, and bootstrapped against their own control pools only exhaustion_short clears P=0.05 (0.033; Holm-adjusted across five gates, 0.166). Previous cycles measured whether the gates made money; this one tried to measure whether they know anything, and came back with not enough evidence to say. That is a weaker claim than Rev1 printed and it is the one the data supports.

The corollary is the one the whole report keeps arriving at from different directions: the money in these runs is a SELECTION problem, not an entry problem. Detection is solved — the tape prints 65 runs a week and something fires near most of them. Nothing we own can tell in advance which ones are worth boarding. That is Movement 3's question.

M3 THE GREENFIELD LAB — build a gate from scratch, then try everything to kill it

Movement 1 found the money and Movement 2 proved the gates we own cannot reach it. This is the from-scratch attempt: 62 sat-out runs, $10,278 of ceiling, and permission to build anything. Everything below was computed this cycle, and it is reported the way this lab always reports — the failures by name, with the test that killed them, because a greenfield lab that only publishes its survivors is a lab that publishes noise.

THE WEEK IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Boarding is not the problem. A deliberately stupid rule — wait for a 5-minute thrust of 1.5×ATR and buy it — fires inside 61 of the 62 runs, a median of 3 minutes late, with a median 45.8 points still to come. Boarded perfectly it is worth $6,050, 58.9% of the whole ceiling. Selection is the problem. That same rule fires 66.4 times a day and only 21.1% of those fires are inside a run. And this week we finally measured why that cannot be fixed with the features we have — see §3, which is the most important result in the movement.

§2  Half the runs have no precursor at all

Split the sat-out runs by whether anything was visible before ignition — a volume z-score, an ATR expansion, an aggressor imbalance:

FamilyRunsCeilingMedian moveMedian vol zMedian ATR expansionUp / Down
A — a precursor is visible31$5,51071 pt2.631.3113 / 18

Two things kill the obvious idea. First, the split is 50/50 — 31 runs show a precursor and 31 show nothing, and the silent half still carries $4,768 of ceiling on a median move of 68 points, which is the same size as the visible half. A precursor filter therefore throws away half the prize before it starts. Second, the precursor is not rare. Across 6,780 minutes, 42.4% of all minutes look like family A — and family A holds 50% of the runs, a lift of just 1.18×.

★ REV2 — THE TABLE ABOVE IS COMPUTED OFF THE DEDUPED RUN LIST, AND THIS SECTION'S OWN APPENDIX SAYS NOT TO DO THAT

The VACUUM appendix (§appendix 1) establishes that run_census.py's keep-strongest dedup selects local extrema — prior-5-minute direction agreement shifts 48.66% → 22.55% across it and the VACUUM rate climbs 10.45% → 14.01% → 21.87% — and it says the finding “invalidates every pre-run price-path statistic quoted off the run list”. §3 obeys that and works on the unselected population. §2 did not. So the same test is re-run here on every minute of the census week whose forward-15-minute move clears the same 55-point threshold, with no dedup: 463 qualifying minutes instead of 62 picked runs, same features, same window. Harness: scripts/rev2_family_unselected.py.

The correction goes the OTHER way, and the conclusion survives it. On the honest population the precursor looks better, not worse — 58.3% of big minutes against a 42.4% base rate, a lift of 1.375× rather than 1.18×. The dedup was working against family A, because a local extremum is the point where the move has already happened and the volume spike is behind it. But the load-bearing half of the finding is untouched: family B is still 193 of 463 (41.7%) of the big minutes, and its median move is 70 points against family A's 71 — on 7× the sample, the silent half is still the same size as the visible half. A 1.375× lift on a feature that fires 42% of the time does not pay for throwing away 42% of the prize.

★★ WHAT TABLES B AND C DO TO TABLE A

Table A is an artefact of not controlling for volatility. A 55-point move is easy on a wide-ATR tape and hard on a quiet one, so anything correlated with ATR — volume, trade count, aggressor flow, all of which are — scores well against a fixed point threshold. It is the same instrument twice.

Normalise the threshold by ATR (B) and the discrimination collapses: ATR expansion falls to 0.234 and ATR level itself to 0.306 — both now worse than a coin flip, i.e. actively anti-predictive. Hold ATR fixed and ask within the band (C) and every feature sits between 0.29 and 0.56.

The desk's entire precursor toolkit measures one thing: how volatile the tape already is. That is genuinely useful — it says a big move is possible now — and it is completely useless for the question we keep asking it, which is which possible move will happen. Three cycles of “selection is the problem” now have a mechanism: we have been feeding the selector a volatility meter and asking it for a direction.

VERDICT — COIL-BRK IS REFUTED

Four independent tests, any one of which is fatal. (1) Out of sample it inverts: in-sample $+3.865/trade, out of sample $−4.615. (2) It is three trades wide: strip its best 3 of 513 and $+2.195/trade becomes $−0.437. (3) The placebo beats it: the same rule taken 30 minutes early — when the coil condition it is built on has not happened yet — books $+3.547/trade against the real signal's $+2.195, and 60 minutes early also beats it. (4) It is a short-side artefact: LONG $−2.051/trade, SHORT $+6.392 — the entire net is one direction on a tape with a known short drift, and it is green on only 22 of 52 days.

Note what the placebo ladder's shape says on its own. The shifted copies decay smoothly from +$3.55 at 30 minutes to −$11.29 at 8 hours. That is not a signal being destroyed by misalignment; it is a slow intraday drift being sampled at different points. The rule is a clock, not a trigger.

★ And the control that settles it: the unarmed break — the same entry with the coil filter switched off entirely — books $+1,625.70 on 1,356 trades ($+1.199/tr) at the 3.0/8.0 exit, against the armed version's $+2.195. The filter this candidate is built around subtracts value. What little is there belongs to the exit geometry, and that is a finding about stops, not about coils.

Moves of 120 points or more are 1.6% of the book — 27 trades of 1,713 — and they carry $8,627 at $319.51 a trade, on a book whose total is $−2,814.00. That is the same conclusion the rider lab and the census reached independently, and it is now three harnesses agreeing.

A 66-trade edge worth 31 cents a trade is not a gate; it is a rounding error with a name.

MOVEMENT 3 — THE BOARD, AND THE VERDICT

Nothing is promoted this week. Nothing is even nominated. One fresh candidate was built and refuted by four independent tests; five frozen candidates were forward-tested and none earned a promotion; the chop-scalp finalist died on its own re-run.

But the movement is not empty, because §3 is a real result and it is structural. For three cycles this lab has closed with “detection is solved, selection is not” without being able to say why selection kept failing. It can now: every precursor feature on this desk is a proxy for ATR, and once ATR is controlled for, all of them fall to a coin flip or below. We have been asking a volatility meter to name a direction. No amount of re-tuning fixes that — it needs an input the desk does not currently record.

★ What that makes actionable is §7, and it needs no new signal at all: 48.2% of entries go nowhere and pay $10 each to find out. Declining the dead band is a size decision, not a direction decision, and it is the one lever in this movement that does not depend on predicting anything.

GREENFIELD — THE CHOP-DAY TURN SCALP (L2-LED)

The short version

Garrath, you asked for a purpose-built chop-turn scalper: catch the oscillation turns on the days the desk currently donates, bank tiny, and lead with the order book — the exhaustion_short lineage, which was built out of L2 footprints and is one of the best things we own.

Last Monday's pass built sixteen candidates and ended with three finalists and a predicted failure: the survivor CT15 looked strong on every conventional test but lost its matched-null comparison, so the write-up called it a search artefact. Four trading days have happened since. This week I ran those three frozen rules on tape that did not exist when they were chosen, and the prediction was right. All three flip sign. Then I searched again on the extended 21-day tape, and the second search dies too — for a reason that is now measured rather than argued.

1. The pre-registered out-of-sample leg kills all three inherited finalists. No re-tuning, no re-fitting, the f_refill median frozen at its original-window value. CT15 goes from +$6.08/trade in-sample to −$2.09 (4 unseen days) and −$6.36 (3 strictly-later days); its win rate collapses 77% → 43%. CT13 +$2.54 → −$0.06/−$0.81. CT16 +$4.27 → +$0.58/−$2.20. The control matters as much as the finalists: the naive chop fade measured −$2.430/trade in-sample and −$2.640 out-of-sample. The loss replicates to within 21 cents. The profit does not replicate at all. That is the signature of an overfit, and it also proves the harness is measuring the same thing on both windows.

2. Your lead hypothesis: I have to correct last week's answer, not confirm it. Last week I told you the absorbing wall actively hurts the fade and "the wall is a target." That does not replicate. On the four new days the sign flips: wall1 ≥ 1.5 drifts −0.118 pt on the original window and +0.393 pt on the new one. It was a one-window read and I stated it too confidently. The honest finding is weaker and duller: no book term, in either window, produces a costed edge — 0 positive cells out of 864 (9 terms × 2 windows × 48 target/stop cells). The one term whose sign is stable across both windows is the inverse of your hypothesis — a thin far side (wall5 ≤ 1.0) drifts +0.273 pt then +0.613 pt — and it too is 0/48 costed.

3. The real cause of death is arithmetic, and I can now put a number on it. Round-trip friction on MNQ is 1.00–1.25 points ($1.50 fee = 0.75 pt, plus the tick we cross on entry, plus the tick a stop slips). I scanned 1,280 filter cells — 32 features × 5 thresholds × 2 directions × 4 horizons — for the best frictionless forward drift any single filter can buy. Best: 1.31 pt. Then I handed the null the identical search, shuffling features within each day: the null's best averages 1.05 pt, and at the 60s and 120s horizons the null BEATS the real tape (p = 0.895, 0.835). A 320-cell search on 4,193 events manufactures roughly as much fake drift as the entire cost barrier is wide. There is no room between the noise floor and the fee.

4. The one cell that cleared both bars still dies costed. CT20 — fade a top-5% 60-second thrust (≥16.75 pt) into a 10-minute extreme — had drift 1.31 pt at t = 2.57, p(null) = 0.065, 131% of friction. Costed across 56 target/stop cells including the tight 0.5R/1R targets you asked for: 0 positive, median −$2.292, best −$0.539.

5. And the premise correction from last week is now sharper, not softer. The desk did not donate on this week's chop day. The tournament took zero trades on 08-24, 08-25, 08-26 and 08-27. Its only trades all week were six legs on Friday 08-28, all winners, +$330.00. Across the full 21-day window the tournament's loss is concentrated in violent-whipsaw blocks (−$1,235.00 on 97 legs, −$12.73/leg) — high ATR going nowhere — not in plain chop (−$403.00 on 58 legs). That is a router bench to price, not a gate for greenfield to build.

On the shuffle p = 0.017. This is exactly the trap last week's study identified, and it is worth being explicit about why the p-value is not a rescue. The shuffle null is a random chop fade, which averages −$2.660/trade. Beating a −$2.66 null with +$0.31 is easy and nearly meaningless; the question was never "is this better than fading at random," it is "is this better than the best cell a search finds in noise" — and §6 answers that with the null's own search, where the null wins at two horizons outright.

Cause of death: leave-one-day-out and strip-the-best. One day or two trades takes it negative, and it loses money on the chop days it was designed for. The out-of-sample sign flip is corroboration.

9. Is the harness real? — the oracle control

A backtester that can only print losses is not evidence of anything. Before the verdict stands, the machinery has to be shown capable of finding money. Same race, same $1.50 round trip, same one-slot sequencing, chop tape, 5/5 target and stop:

The oracle must win, and it does, decisively and symmetrically. The harness finds money when money is there. The negative chop numbers are a finding, not a bug.

Null reported for completeness: I also tried an honest non-look-ahead positive control — trend-continuation on TREND-daytype days — and it returned n = 6. TREND regime blocks are only 47 of the 946 blocks in the window (5.0%), and requiring a ≥4 pt 60-second thrust through an extreme inside one, on a TREND-typed day, leaves six events. The control is unpowered and returns no verdict either way. I am not counting its negative sign as evidence of anything.

10. The arithmetic against your +$200–300 bar

Median 30-minute CHOP block range across the 535 chop blocks in the 21 full-stack days: 45.50 points (50.50 pt across all 31 day-files of bars — I use the tighter, matched number here).

This is the tension, and it is arithmetic rather than opinion. You asked for selectivity — "a few high-quality turns a day, not hundreds" — and selectivity and the dollar target pull in opposite directions. At 3.8 fires a day CT13 needs to capture 72% of an entire 30-minute range on every single trade. At 199 fires a day the naive fade needs only $1.26 a trade — a bar so low it sounds trivial — and it measures −$2.24, because 199 round trips a day is a $298.80 daily fee tax before a single point of edge.

The best $/trade found anywhere in the entire R-sweep is +$0.311. At that rate +$250 a day requires 804 trades. There is no point on this curve that reaches your bar.

12. What I would actually do with this

1. Stop trying to build a chop-turn scalper on MNQ at this fee. Not because the turns are random — they are not; unfiltered chop turns drift +0.09 to +0.34 pt in the fade's favour, and the oracle shows $615.50 a chop day sitting there. Because the drift is a fifth to a third of the round trip, and the search noise floor on this event count is the same width as the barrier. To clear it you would need a filter buying >1.25 pt of drift that is not a search artefact, and 1,280 cells did not produce one.

2. The premise itself is the actionable finding, and it is now two weeks old and unmoved. The tournament does not donate on chop days — this week it did not trade four of five days at all. It donates in WHIPSAW: −$1,235.00 on 97 legs at −$12.73/leg, versus −$403.00 on 58 legs in plain chop. That is a router bench with a defined trigger — high atr_rel with low ER — and it is worth 3.1× more than anything a chop scalper could recover. I would price that bench before building anything new. It is the same recommendation as last week, and four more days have strengthened it.

3. If you want one more swing at the book, swing at the opposite of what we assumed. The only book term with a stable sign across both windows is the thin far side (wall5 ≤ 1.0: +0.273 pt then +0.613 pt), not the absorbing one. It is 0/48 costed and I am not recommending it as a candidate — but if the L2 lead is revisited, "price ran out of tape" is the hypothesis with two consistent reads behind it, and "the far side is absorbing" now has two contradictory ones.

4. Two corrections to carry forward. Last week's "the wall is a target" was a one-window read and does not replicate — please don't let it become desk lore. And the exhaustion_short lineage cannot be ported to chop tape: its 400-contract aggressor floor plus stall plus wall occurs once in five chop days.

13. What would change this verdict

Stated in advance so it is falsifiable rather than a hedge:

  • A filter buying > 1.25 pt of frictionless drift with n ≥ 100 that survives the matched-null search (not a single-cell shuffle). Nothing in 1,280 cells got there.
  • More chop days. Five in the full-stack window is thin, and the 30s horizon's p = 0.065 is a near-miss I would happily re-test on twenty chop days rather than five. The lake grows ~5 days a week; this is worth re-running at ~40 full-stack days.
  • A lower fee. At $1.50 the round trip the barrier is 1.00–1.25 pt. Everything here is a statement about that number, not about the tape.
  • A different instrument. MGC is $10.00/point, so the identical $1.50 fee is 0.15 pt of friction rather than 0.75 — one fifth. The entire arithmetic in §10 changes sign-of-feasibility on gold. That is out of this section's scope and belongs to gf_MGC, but it follows directly from §6 and I would not want it lost.
VERDICT

IT DID NOT SURVIVE. The three inherited finalists were killed by the pre-registered out-of-sample leg — CT15 +$6.077 → −$2.091 (wide) / −$6.357 (strict), CT13 +$2.541 → −$0.059 / −$0.808, CT16 +$4.265 → +$0.583 / −$2.200 — while the naive-fade control replicated its loss to within $0.21, confirming the split measures the same thing on both sides. The fresh 21-day search was killed by the matched-null test: its best cell bought 1.315 pt of drift where the null's own search bought 1.050 pt on shuffled features (p = 0.065), and at the 60s and 120s horizons the null beat the real tape outright (p = 0.895, 0.835). The one candidate that cleared both the friction barrier and its null, CT20, was killed by the costed grid — 0 of 56 cells positive, best −$0.539/trade, including the 0.5R and 1R targets requested. The single positive cell left in the entire study, CT13 at 6/8, was killed by leave-one-day-out and strip-the-best-trades: dropping one day of twenty takes it to −$0.347/trade and stripping two trades of sixty-six takes it to −$0.008, and it loses $28.50 at −$1.500/trade on the five chop days it was built for. No candidate was killed on win rate — CT20's costed cells win 59–73% and are still negative. The harness passes its oracle control at +$3.29/trade, so these are findings and not artefacts. Nothing here is fit to arm, shadow, or paper-trade.

A2–A6 — THE FOUR CLUSTER HUNTS THE ROTATION DID NOT SCHEDULE THIS WEEK

The serial runner logged, at 22:14:21Z: ROTATION (ISO week 35): running 2 of 6 greenfield clusters. NOT run this week: gf_OPEN-NEWS, gf_RIDER_ALL, gf_UNCLASS, gf_VACUUM. This is the design working, not a failure — six cluster hunts at ~25 minutes each do not fit in one Friday night, so they rotate and each is re-run roughly every three weeks.

Their dossiers are reproduced below as a standing reference, dated 2026-08-22 and 2026-08-25. They are NOT this week's work and nothing on the action card rests on them. What IS this week's work is §5 above, which takes every candidate these four labs produced, on the specs they were frozen with, and prices them forward on tape they had never seen. That is the honest way to carry a rotated-out lab: freeze the claim, then grade it.

THE POOLED RUN-CATCHER — one rider for every sat-out run NOT RUN THIS WEEK · dossier 2026-08-25

Board any run late, ride it wide, filter it causally.

GREENFIELD SYNTHESIS — ONE RIDER FOR EVERY SAT-OUT RUN

MNQ · full parquet lake (5s bars 2026-07-16 → 08-24) + a 236-session out-of-sample leg · $2.00/point · $1.50 per round trip
THE SHORT VERSION, BEFORE ANY OF THE WORKING

Garrath — I built the direction-agnostic run-catcher you asked for, boarded it late exactly as the gold work suggested, swept the exit far wider than the desk has ever run one, filtered it with a causal rule, and put the survivor through the whole battery. It passed every in-sample test we have, including two separate placebo controls. Then it died on the out-of-sample leg, and it died again on a live shadow arm that has been quietly recording forward trades since Monday.

It died at STEP 3 — the causal filter. The test that killed it was the out-of-sample leg: 1,289 trades over 236 untouched sessions for a total of +$14. Not a loss. Not a win. Nothing. The 95% confidence interval on its expectancy runs from −0.204R to +0.246R per trade, which is another way of saying we measured zero with a wide ruler.

And there is a second, independent witness that agrees, which is the part you should trust most. rider_w5 — the board arm this desk shipped into the shadow book on 2026-08-15 off last week's version of this very phase, quoted then at +$4,841 and +$19.29 a trade — has taken 51 forward trades since 08-17 and sits at −$1,471, or −$28.84 a trade, red on six of seven days and red in every single ATR bucket. Nobody had graded it. This section grades it.

Three things came out of the week that are worth more than the failed rider:

  1. The $9,610 is not $9,610. Even a perfect late boarder — one that fires inside all 62 runs at a median three minutes in and then exits at the exact top of the move with no costs at all — can only reach $5,094, or 53% of the ceiling. Thirteen per cent of the runs are already finished by the time any honest detector can see them. The number the census puts on the table is a hindsight number and the rider's half of it is gone before we start.
  2. Detection is not our problem and never was. A five-minute boarding trigger fires inside 62 of 62 sat-out runs at a median of three minutes late, with a median 41 points still ahead. It also fires 34 times a day on tape that goes nowhere. The gap is selection, not detection — which is exactly what the greenfield census concluded from the other direction.
  3. I found a backtest bug that was manufacturing a winner, and it is the kind that would have shipped. Details in §3. The whole chandelier family survived every robustness test I have until I fixed it, and then went from +$4,270 to −$631.

Full verdict, dispositions and the one shadow proposal are at the bottom. Every dead candidate is named with its cause of death.

0. THE ANCHOR — I REPRODUCED THE FROZEN CENSUS BEFORE TOUCHING ANYTHING

I did not re-run run_census.py. I re-derived its run set from the lake with its own algorithm and checked it line by line against the frozen census_stdout.txt.

⚠ The brief I was handed says "60 runs, $8,025". That is last week's census. This week's frozen file says 62 runs and $9,610, and since the frozen file is the contract, every number below is scored against $9,610. Worth flagging because the two numbers are close enough to pass unnoticed.

One small defect found in the census while anchoring to it. The census slides its 15-minute window by array index, not by clock. Where the 5s tape has holes the two drift apart, and only 16 of the 62 sat-out run timestamps are actually minute-aligned — the offsets run 10s, 15s, 25s … up to 55s. It changes no money, but a run in that table is located to about ±1 minute, not to the second, and anything that joins to those timestamps on an exact match will silently miss most of them. I snapped each run to the minute bar containing it and took start prices from the 5s bar at the exact census timestamp.

1. STEP ONE — BOARD IT. WHEN COULD WE HAVE KNOWN, AND WHAT WAS LEFT?

The instruction was to stop trying to predict a run and instead board it after it has proven itself, then measure what remains. On gold that shape fired a median 19 minutes into the top five runs with about 80% of the move still ahead. Here is the same curve for MNQ.

The boarding rule is deliberately dumb and direction-agnostic: at each completed one-minute bar, take the net move over the trailing W minutes; if it is at least k × ATR and the efficiency ratio over that window is at least e, board it in whichever direction the move went. ATR here is the mean one-minute high-low range over the last 20 minutes, which is the exact number the live router already prints, so anything built on it is deployable as written.

"What was left" is measured to the run's own terminus — the furthest the move got before giving back a full ATR — with no costs and no stop. It is a pure oracle: this is the most any rider could have taken, not what one would take.

Read the top row properly, because it is the most encouraging number in this whole section and it is still not enough. A five-minute confirmation catches every one of the 62 runs we sat out, and it catches them fast — three minutes in at the median, ten minutes at the very worst. At that moment the median run still has 41 points and 63% of its move in front of it. Detection latency, on this trigger, is simply not the problem.

That directly contradicts the prior this desk has been carrying. Part 2.5's detection-latency finding — median 119 points already moved, median 16 points left, 12% capture — was measured on a 30-minute window with net ≥ 80 and ER ≥ 0.35. That is a much heavier confirmation and it buys a much later seat. Shortening the window from 30 minutes to 5 moves the median from "16 points left" to "41 points left". The latency was a property of the instrument we were measuring with, not of the tape.

Now the two hard limits the same table imposes:

  • 13% of runs have nothing left at all. By the time even the fastest honest trigger fires, the move is done. Those runs are not catchable by any boarding strategy, only by a predicting one, and predicting run starts is already a banked null on 22.6M ticks.
  • The oracle ceiling is 53%, not 100%. $5,094 of the $9,610, with a cheating exit and zero costs. Tighten the trigger to something you would actually trade and it falls to 20–24%. Every honest conversation about this money should start from about $2,000–$5,000 a week, not $9,610.

And the thing the table does not show: that same W=5 / k=1.0 trigger fires 34 times a day. Over the 35-day lake it produces 1,180 boards, of which about 60 a month are these runs. The other 96% are ordinary tape. That is the whole problem, and it is where the rest of this section goes.

2. STEP TWO — THE EXIT. SWEPT WIDE, AND THEN SWEPT AGAIN ON A SAMPLE TEN TIMES BIGGER

The instruction was explicit: sweep the exit wide before concluding any entry fails, because three separate results this week said a tight exit gets shaken out of a grind while the same entries with a wide stop and a far target make money.

I did that first on the 35-day 5s lake. Entry set held fixed (W=8, k=1.5, ER≥0.50, 60-minute lockout, 1,034 boards) so that every cell differs in the exit and nothing else.

Hold-to-time-cap variants (no target, flat at 15 / 30 / 60 / 240 minutes) were negative almost everywhere — that column is the right-hand edge of the table above.

⚠ THE GRAVE THAT MATTERS MOST — a backtest bug that manufactured a winner

The chandelier family — wide stop, trail armed after N×ATR, give back k×ATR from the peak — came out of this sweep looking like the answer. It was the only exit family positive in nearly every regime cell across two different entry definitions, and chand_2.5_a1.5_t1.5 on the W=10 entry set survived everything I threw at it: +$4,270 net, +$4.58 a trade, 60% win, strip-best-3 still +$3,115, strip-best-10 still +$1,098, day-green 61%, worst day −$631.

It was wrong. My trail was testing the bar's HIGH against the running peak instead of its LOW. A 5s bar that printed a new high and then collapsed registered a give-back of exactly zero, so the trail never fired inside the bar that actually broke it — it exited later, at prices that never traded. The peak was also read including the current bar, which is a second look-ahead on top of the first.

The tell was there before I found it, and it is worth naming so we catch the next one faster: the random-entry placebo. Firing at completely random minutes in a random direction with that same chandelier made +$1,542 on average, and the "real" rider's +$4,270 sat at p = 0.115 against that null. A random entry should not make money. When your null hypothesis starts printing, the bug is in the machinery, not in the market.

Fixed — peak taken from strictly prior bars, give-back tested against the adverse edge — here is what happened to the whole family:

chand 3.0 / arm 2 / trail 2W=8 k1.5+$3,026−$1,471
chand 4.0 / arm 2 / trail 3W=8 k1.5+$5,247 (strip-10 −$736)−$872 (strip-10 −$6,748)

Every single one flipped. Not one chandelier configuration in the study is positive with a correct trail. Cause of death: a backtest bug, self-inflicted, caught by the placebo control. Everything below this line uses the fixed simulator.

The honest sweep — every cell judged, not just the best one

Cherry-picking the best cell out of a grid is how a desk convinces itself. So I ran the full grid — 5 entry windows × 6 thresholds × 4 ER floors × 2 lockouts × 8 exits = 1,824 scored cells — and put the same battery on every one of them: net > 0, strip-best-3 > 0, strip-best-10 > 0, and both halves of the tape positive, with n ≥ 60.

barcells passingshare
